questions.stem: A healthy patient completed a phone preanesthesia interview 12 days ago. The chart is complete and nothing has changed. Which requirement still cannot be omitted on the morning of surgery?
options: A repeat interview only if laboratory values changed
No further interview because the phone assessment remains valid
An in-person clinic interview because the prior assessment was remote
questions.explanation: A preanesthesia assessment may be done days to weeks ahead, including by phone, but a day-of-surgery interview is still required to confirm identity, NPO status, medications taken, and any interval change before anesthesia. A remote assessment is valid, so an in-person clinic visit is not required, and the morning check is not limited to changed labs.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A 58-year-old has well-controlled hypertension, type 2 diabetes on metformin without complications, and BMI 36. Which ASA physical status is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: ASA II describes mild systemic disease without substantive functional limitation, such as well-controlled hypertension or diabetes and obesity with a BMI between 30 and 40. ASA III requires severe systemic disease with functional limitation, such as poorly controlled diabetes or BMI of 40 or more, and ASA IV is a constant threat to life.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: An elective colectomy patient has EF 25%, stage 4 CKD, and insulin-dependent diabetes but is not acutely decompensated. What timing best preserves an opportunity for optimization rather than merely identifying risk on the day of surgery?
options: At least a week before surgery
Any time within 30 days if symptoms develop
questions.explanation: Medically complex patients should visit the preop testing center at least a week before surgery so testing and optimization can happen and preventable cancellations are avoided.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A hospital is deciding whether an in-person preoperative testing clinic adds value beyond a day-of-surgery interview. Which benefits justify the clinic? (Select 4)
options: Consolidated testing such as labs, imaging, and other studies
Time to optimize medical conditions before surgery
Replacement of the surgeon's history and physical
questions.explanation: An in-person preoperative clinic allows patient education that lowers anxiety, consolidates testing, gives time to optimize medical conditions, and reduces preventable day-of-surgery cancellations. It does not eliminate the day-of-surgery interview, since conditions can change, and it does not replace the surgeon's history and physical.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A 66-year-old takes metoprolol, lisinopril for hypertension, furosemide for uncomplicated hypertension, and glipizide. Which medication is most consistently continued on the morning of surgery to avoid withdrawal-related tachycardia and ischemia?
questions.explanation: Chronic beta-blockers are generally continued perioperatively because abrupt withdrawal can cause tachycardia and ischemia. Management of renin-angiotensin system inhibitors and diuretics depends on indication, patient status, and procedural risk; oral sulfonylureas are withheld while fasting.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient takes losartan for uncomplicated hypertension, amlodipine, and hydrochlorothiazide and is scheduled for major surgery with expected fluid shifts. Which plan is most consistent with limiting peri-induction hypotension while maintaining needed antihypertensive therapy?
options: Take amlodipine; hold losartan and hydrochlorothiazide
Take losartan; hold amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide
Take hydrochlorothiazide and amlodipine; hold losartan
questions.explanation: Amlodipine is generally continued. For a patient taking an ARB for hypertension who is undergoing higher-risk surgery, withholding it before surgery may reduce intraoperative hypotension; a thiazide may also be withheld when fasting or volume depletion is a concern. ARBs used for heart failure require separate individualized consideration.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A 68-year-old taking lisinopril for hypertension takes the usual dose on the morning of major surgery. After induction, BP falls to 68/35 and responds poorly to phenylephrine. Which mechanism can contribute to this pattern?
questions.explanation: ACE inhibition reduces angiotensin II formation, removing a major compensatory vasoconstrictor pathway during anesthetic vasodilation, so hypotension after induction can be severe and respond poorly to phenylephrine; vasopressin is often effective. This is why continuation is individualized by indication and surgical risk.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: One patient has a drug-eluting coronary stent and takes aspirin plus clopidogrel; another takes rivaroxaban for atrial fibrillation. Which management principle applies to both before surgery?
options: Hold both drug classes only on the morning of surgery as a fixed rule
Continue both drug classes through surgery as a fixed rule
Individualize interruption or continuation by balancing bleeding and thrombosis
Replace either regimen with low-dose aspirin the day before surgery
questions.explanation: Antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy is managed case by case, weighing surgical and neuraxial bleeding risk against thrombotic risk such as stent thrombosis or stroke. A recent drug-eluting stent may need dual antiplatelet therapy continued, while rivaroxaban is usually held for a set interval based on renal function. Fixed rules or substituting aspirin ignore that balance.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient with Parkinson disease and a seizure disorder is NPO for surgery and asks whether carbidopa-levodopa and levetiracetam should be skipped. Which instruction best prevents avoidable perioperative deterioration?
options: Hold both to minimize anesthetic interactions
Take both on the morning of surgery
questions.explanation: Abrupt interruption of levetiracetam can permit breakthrough seizures, while missed carbidopa-levodopa can rapidly worsen rigidity and mobility and may impair airway protection. These chronic neurologic medications are therefore generally maintained as close to the normal schedule as possible.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A 70-year-old takes furosemide, glyburide, a multivitamin, fish oil, an albuterol inhaler, and metoprolol. Which four are ordinarily held on the morning of surgery? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: On the morning of surgery, diuretics such as furosemide are usually held to avoid hypovolemia and hypokalemia, oral hypoglycemics such as glyburide are held to prevent hypoglycemia while fasting, and vitamins and fish oil are held because they add nothing and some affect bleeding. Inhalers and beta-blockers are continued.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient takes oxycodone 10 mg every 8 hours chronically and is scheduled for a painful laminectomy. Which morning-of-surgery instruction best limits withdrawal and worsening postoperative analgesic requirements?
options: Hold the dose to reduce intraoperative respiratory depression
Take half of the usual dose
Hold the dose and substitute only a postoperative PCA
questions.explanation: Chronic opioid therapy produces physical dependence and tolerance. Continuing the baseline opioid helps prevent withdrawal and supplies the patient's usual opioid requirement; the surgical analgesic plan must then treat additional postoperative pain on top of that baseline.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: Which preoperative action best reflects the purpose of evaluation rather than simply completing documentation?
options: Diagnose every untreated disease, order routine labs, and schedule surgery
Identify modifiable risk, prepare the patient, and build an anesthetic plan
Obtain consent, administer premedication, and start an IV
Assign ASA class, calculate one risk score, and determine staffing
questions.explanation: Preoperative evaluation exists to identify modifiable risk, prepare the patient medically and psychologically, and build an anesthetic plan that reduces morbidity, not just to complete forms. Routine testing, consent, premedication, and a single risk score are parts of the process rather than its purpose.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: You begin chart review for the first case of the day. Which verification comes before interpreting comorbidities, laboratory values, or prior anesthetic records?
options: The most recent laboratory values and imaging
Risk stratification and the provisional anesthetic plan
Patient identity and the planned procedure
questions.explanation: Chart review starts by confirming the patient's identity and the planned procedure, because labs, records, and risk assessment are useless if they belong to the wrong patient or case. After that comes history, prior anesthetic records, labs, risk stratification, consent, allergies, and medications. The surgeon's preference does not come first.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A prior anesthetic record documents a grade 4 laryngoscopic view with successful bougie-assisted video laryngoscopy. What should this finding change before induction?
options: Choose regional anesthesia solely to avoid airway management
Document it but begin with the usual airway plan
Use rapid-sequence induction with a Mac 4 blade as the default first attempt
Prepare a difficult-airway strategy and equipment in advance
questions.explanation: Identifying previous intubation notes and difficult airways is a chart review essential. It should drive equipment and plan, such as VL and the difficult airway cart.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A 72-year-old reports severe postoperative nausea and vomiting and two days of confusion after a prior anesthetic. Which additional anesthesia-history elements belong in the same focused review? (Select 4)
options: Personal or family history of malignant hyperthermia
questions.explanation: A focused anesthesia history asks about prior PONV, emergence delirium or delayed emergence, personal or family history of malignant hyperthermia, and prior difficult airway, because each changes the current plan. Prior responses to regional anesthesia can matter, but the surgeon's name does not.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient's father developed marked hyperthermia and muscle rigidity during anesthesia and nearly died. Which interpretation has the greatest anesthetic consequence?
options: Social history pointing to alcohol withdrawal
Anesthesia history suggesting familial MH risk
questions.explanation: Hyperthermia and rigidity during a parent's anesthetic suggest malignant hyperthermia, an autosomal dominant condition, so the patient is treated as MH-susceptible unless testing shows otherwise, with a trigger-free anesthetic and dantrolene available. Pseudocholinesterase deficiency causes prolonged paralysis, not hyperthermia.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: The chart lists no prior anesthetic complications, but the patient recalls awakening after surgery, becoming severely dyspneic, and requiring reintubation. What is the most important lesson for the current evaluation?
options: Key complications may be missing from the chart
The patient likely misremembers the event
Recalled events matter only if documented
Charts are complete for prior anesthetics
questions.explanation: The interview often reveals complications, such as reintubation, that never reached the available record, so patient recall is taken seriously and records are sought. Dismissing the memory or trusting the chart as complete risks repeating a dangerous event.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: One patient lists codeine as an allergy because of nausea and pruritus; another reports penicillin-associated hives and lip swelling. What distinction should be explicitly documented because it changes how each entry is interpreted?
questions.explanation: The reaction phenotype matters more than simply recording an allergy label. Hives and angioedema support an immune-mediated hypersensitivity history, whereas nausea and some opioid-associated pruritus are adverse effects rather than proof of allergy; distinguishing them prevents both unsafe re-exposure and unnecessary drug avoidance.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: You have limited time for a focused day-of-surgery examination before an uncomplicated hernia repair. Which examination set is most aligned with anesthesia-specific risk detection?
options: Airway, pulmonary, hematologic, renal, and skin
Airway, cardiovascular, renal, skin, and musculoskeletal
Neurologic, cardiovascular, endocrine, renal, and gastrointestinal
Airway, neurologic, cardiovascular, pulmonary, and gastrointestinal
questions.explanation: The focused day-of-surgery examination concentrates on the airway, neurologic, cardiovascular, pulmonary, and gastrointestinal systems because they most directly affect airway management, hemodynamic response, ventilation, and aspiration risk. Skin, renal, and musculoskeletal findings are noted when relevant but are not the core set.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient had a complete preoperative clinic examination two weeks ago but now reports new bilateral ankle swelling. What is required before induction?
options: No exam, since the clinic physical stands
A focused exam addressing the new swelling
A repeat full physical if labs have changed
questions.explanation: A day-of-surgery focused exam of the airway, heart, lungs, and relevant systems is done even after a recent clinic visit, and new bilateral ankle edema needs assessment for heart failure or volume overload before induction. A two-week-old physical does not cover the change, and cancellation is decided only after the patient is examined.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A healthy ambulatory patient's friend will drive them home after anesthesia and then leave, and the patient lives alone. Which discharge issue should be identified before proceeding?
options: A driver meets the discharge needs
A taxi ride home would be acceptable
No adult can stay for the first 24 hours
questions.explanation: After anesthesia and sedation, outpatients need a responsible adult to drive them home and to stay with them, usually for the first 24 hours, because judgment and coordination may be impaired. A driver alone or a taxi does not meet that need, and the gap can often be solved by arranging a caregiver rather than mandatory admission.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: The chart already documents OSA on CPAP, diabetes, and a previous difficult intubation. With limited preoperative interview time, which approach best reduces the chance of missing a new risk?
options: Verify known risks, then probe for gaps
Ask only about diagnoses already in the chart
Repeat the entire history without the chart
Skip questions about systems that seem unchanged
questions.explanation: With limited time, confirming the documented high-risk findings first and then deliberately asking about interval changes and missing information balances efficiency with completeness. Asking only about charted diagnoses misses new problems, and ignoring the chart wastes time.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: An SRNA repeatedly omits important preoperative questions when cases become busy. Which change most directly reduces omission errors without replacing clinical judgment?
options: Substitute a patient questionnaire for the interview
Use a scripted consent video before each case
Rely on the preoperative order set to capture the history
Use a consistent structured interview template
questions.explanation: A consistent, structured interview template reduces omissions when cases are busy while still leaving room for clinical judgment, which is why one is recommended early in training. Questionnaires, consent videos, and order sets support the process but do not replace a complete interview.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient appears guarded at the start of the preoperative interview. Which opening approach is most likely to improve disclosure without sacrificing professionalism?
options: Begin with rapid closed questions first
Introduce yourself, your role, and the purpose
Use a nickname from the chart to seem close
Explain your role later, during consent
questions.explanation: Introducing yourself and your role, addressing the patient respectfully, often by surname, and explaining why the interview matters builds trust, which improves disclosure and the quality of consent. Rapid questioning before introductions or unasked-for nicknames can increase guardedness.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient with normal renal function takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation. Under ASRA guidance, how long before a planned spinal should the last dose be taken?
questions.explanation: ASRA guidance recommends stopping direct factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban and rivaroxaban 72 hours before neuraxial puncture or catheter removal, longer with renal impairment, to limit the risk of spinal epidural hematoma. Twelve or 24 hours is too short, and 7 days applies to drugs such as clopidogrel, not apixaban.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: Three weeks before elective hip replacement, a patient reports exertional chest pain and subsequent testing demonstrates inducible ischemia. Which function of the preoperative process is most clearly demonstrated?
options: Replacing the surgeon's history and physical
Improving room turnover by testing early
Finding a problem in time to optimize
questions.explanation: Exertional chest pain found three weeks before elective surgery, with ischemia on testing, shows the preoperative process identifying a problem early enough for cardiology evaluation and possible treatment before surgery. It does not replace the surgeon's H&P, and turnover and discharge planning are secondary goals.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A fasting patient accidentally takes the usual morning glipizide dose before surgery. Which immediate preoperative risk should receive priority surveillance?
questions.explanation: Sulfonylureas stimulate insulin secretion even when the patient is not eating. Taking glipizide while fasting can therefore produce perioperative hypoglycemia, making immediate glucose assessment and continued surveillance the priority.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A preoperative holding RN obtains an excellent history and airway screen. What remains necessary before anesthesia under the facility's stated assessment policy?
options: An authorized anesthesia or advanced provider
The RN screen suffices for ASA I and II
A later cosign makes the RN screen formal
The surgeon's review of the RN screen
questions.explanation: The formal preanesthesia assessment must be performed by a clinician authorized under facility policy, such as an anesthesiologist, CRNA, NP, or PA, even when a nurse has collected an excellent history and airway screen. A cosign or surgeon review does not convert the nursing assessment into the anesthesia evaluation.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A chart carries a difficult-airway alert, but the patient cannot recall details. Which two previous-record findings would be most useful before finalizing the airway plan? (Select 2)
options: Documentation of mask ventilation or supraglottic-airway difficulty
Previous laryngoscopic view and device used for intubation
questions.explanation: Prior airway records can show the laryngoscopic view and device that worked, and whether mask or supraglottic ventilation was difficult, which directly shape the primary and rescue plans. Postoperative opioid use, induction drug, sore throat, and position may be noted but do not define the airway plan.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient reports that after a prior anesthetic he became apneic in PACU and required prolonged respiratory support. Which preoperative interpretation is most appropriate?
options: A medication issue from benzodiazepines only
An anesthesia history signal such as OSA
Social history pointing to substance misuse
Surgical history, since it followed surgery
questions.explanation: Postoperative apnea requiring prolonged support is part of the anesthesia history and raises concern for undiagnosed OSA or heightened sensitivity to opioids and sedatives, which changes analgesia, monitoring, and the postoperative setting. Labeling it as a single drug effect, social history, or surgical history misses that implication.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: An 81-year-old was confused and not at baseline for three days after a previous anesthetic. Where should this information be captured because it may alter the current anesthetic and recovery plan?
options: Medication history as an opioid side effect
questions.explanation: Postoperative delirium or delayed recovery after a previous anesthetic belongs in the anesthesia history because it predicts recurrence, especially in older adults, and prompts delirium prevention such as avoiding benzodiazepines and anticholinergics, limiting depth, and optimizing analgesia. Filing it as a medication side effect hides its significance.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient has never received anesthesia and reports no known drug allergies. How should this history affect planning?
options: Low reaction risk means allergy need not be verified
Raise the ASA class because exposure is unknown
Avoid common anesthetic drugs on first exposure
Do not assume tolerance; stay ready for reactions
questions.explanation: A patient who has never had anesthesia has no history of tolerating its drugs, so the absence of known allergy does not prove a reaction will not occur; allergy history is still verified and standard readiness for anaphylaxis maintained. First exposure does not change ASA class or require avoiding common drugs.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: An 84-year-old with a mechanical mitral valve takes warfarin and presents with a hip fracture and INR 3.1. Which approach best reflects the competing perioperative risks?
options: Coordinate reversal, timing, and thrombosis protection
Continue warfarin and treat any bleeding later
Stop warfarin and proceed without further planning
Replace warfarin with aspirin and then proceed
questions.explanation: A mechanical mitral valve carries high thromboembolic risk, while an INR of 3.1 makes surgery and neuraxial anesthesia unsafe, so reversal with vitamin K or prothrombin complex concentrate, timing, and bridging are planned with surgery and cardiology. Aspirin does not protect a mechanical valve.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient was considered low risk three weeks ago, but this morning potassium is 6.1 mEq/L with new peaked T waves. What must the day-of-surgery review do first with the prior assessment?
options: Confirm only that the surgical consent is signed
Recheck whether the prior plan is still valid
Confirm NPO status and keep the prior plan
Accept the plan, since it is within 30 days
questions.explanation: New hyperkalemia with peaked T waves is a dangerous interval change, so the day-of-surgery review asks whether the earlier risk assessment and plan still apply; usually the potassium is treated and its cause found before an elective case proceeds, and succinylcholine is avoided. A plan made three weeks earlier does not account for it.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient with a family history suggestive of malignant hyperthermia wants to know whether they are susceptible. Which test is the reference standard?
questions.explanation: The caffeine-halothane contracture test on a fresh muscle biopsy is the reference standard for MH susceptibility; genetic testing for RYR1 or CACNA1S variants can confirm susceptibility but a negative result does not exclude it. Resting CK is nonspecific, and the dibucaine number and cholinesterase activity evaluate succinylcholine metabolism, not MH.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient with atrial fibrillation misses the usual morning metoprolol dose and arrives with HR 118/min. Which consequence best explains why chronic beta-blocker therapy is ordinarily continued?
options: Lower MAC from stopping the beta-blocker
Lost rate control with rebound sympathetic tone
questions.explanation: Chronic beta-blockade upregulates beta receptors, so a missed dose leads to rebound sympathetic activity, loss of rate control, tachycardia, and increased myocardial oxygen demand that can provoke ischemia. That is why beta-blockers are continued the morning of surgery. Withdrawal does not lower MAC or prolong neuromuscular blockade.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient consents to general anesthesia with an LMA after hearing only the planned technique; possible intubation and neuraxial alternatives were not discussed. Which element of informed consent is deficient?
options: Meaningful discussion of material risks and reasonable alternatives
The consent was signed after, rather than before, the discussion
Regional anesthesia is not an alternative that needs discussion
Airway risks are covered automatically by the surgical consent
questions.explanation: Informed consent requires a discussion of material risks, benefits, and reasonable alternatives, so a patient consenting to an LMA should hear that intubation may be needed and that neuraxial or regional options exist when appropriate. Surgical consent does not cover anesthesia risks, and timing of the signature does not fix a missing discussion.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient with severe COPD is scheduled for total knee arthroplasty. Which anesthetic option deserves explicit discussion because it may reduce the need for airway instrumentation and systemic respiratory depressants?
options: Deep sedation without a secured airway
questions.explanation: For a patient with severe COPD having knee arthroplasty, neuraxial or regional anesthesia can avoid airway instrumentation, bronchospasm triggers, and systemic respiratory depressants, so it deserves explicit discussion. An LMA still requires general anesthesia, and deep sedation risks hypoventilation without airway control.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: After evaluating a patient with OSA and coronary disease for colectomy, which three decisions belong directly in the anesthesia plan generated from the assessment? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: The preoperative assessment drives anesthesia decisions such as medication management, monitoring, and positioning and equipment, for example CPAP availability and opioid-sparing analgesia for OSA and ischemia monitoring for CAD. Incision, surgical approach, and length of stay are surgical or system decisions.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient takes St. John's wort, ginkgo, and vitamin E before a spine procedure. Which instruction best addresses medication-interaction and bleeding concerns?
options: Take half-doses on the morning of surgery
Continue all three to prevent withdrawal
Hold the vitamins and herbal products before surgery
Continue ginkgo but hold St. John's wort and vitamin E
questions.explanation: Vitamins and herbal supplements are usually held before surgery: ginkgo and high-dose vitamin E can increase bleeding, which matters for spine surgery, and St. John's wort induces CYP enzymes and interacts with many anesthetic drugs. Herbal products are commonly stopped 1 to 2 weeks ahead when possible.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: During preoperative interview, a patient discloses hepatitis C and prior IV drug use that were not documented in the chart. Which risk-assessment function is most directly served by obtaining this history?
options: Exposure risk to patient and team
questions.explanation: Disclosing hepatitis C and prior IV drug use identifies bloodborne pathogen exposure risk to the team and informs patient risks such as liver disease. It may also affect ASA class or disposition, but the most direct function is recognizing exposure risk so standard precautions and sharps safety are reinforced.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient with limited English proficiency needs to give consent for anesthesia, and an adult child offers to interpret. What is the best approach?
options: Let the adult child interpret for consent
Proceed in English if the patient nods
Ask the surgeon to obtain all consent
questions.explanation: Consent requires that the patient understand risks, benefits, and alternatives, so a qualified medical interpreter, in person or remote, is used; family members may filter or misstate information and add privacy problems. Nodding does not show understanding, and the surgeon's consent does not cover anesthesia.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for ankle fixation under a popliteal block with minimal sedation. Which reason best justifies performing the same airway assessment used before general anesthesia?
options: Regional or MAC plans can fail or deepen
Airway findings set the local anesthetic dose
Fracture blocks fail more often than others
questions.explanation: A block can fail, sedation can deepen, or LAST or another complication can occur, any of which may require airway rescue or conversion to general anesthesia, so the airway is assessed before every anesthetic. Sedation does not mandate intubation, and airway findings do not determine local anesthetic dose.

questions.stem: A patient has Mallampati II, adequate mouth opening, a full beard, a short thick neck, and limited cervical extension. Which interpretation is most useful for planning?
options: The beard by itself decides the airway plan
Modest predictors can combine into difficulty
Mallampati II makes the others unimportant
Neck extension by itself decides the plan
questions.explanation: A beard, short thick neck, and limited extension each modestly predict difficulty, but together they can make both mask ventilation and laryngoscopy hard even with a Mallampati II view, so the plan accounts for the combination. No single predictor is reliable on its own.

questions.stem: A patient with BMI 38, Mallampati III, a full beard, and a short neck requires general anesthesia. Which preparation best matches the combined airway findings without overcommitting to one technique?
options: Delay surgery until the beard is shaved
Standard setup, since no single sign is certain
Optimized positioning, VL, and rescue equipment
Awake fiberoptic for every such patient
questions.explanation: BMI 38, Mallampati III, a beard, and a short neck together predict difficult mask ventilation and laryngoscopy, so ramped positioning, video laryngoscopy, adjuncts, and difficult-airway rescue equipment are prepared. Awake intubation is reserved for higher predicted difficulty or aspiration risk, and a beard alone is not a reason to delay.

questions.stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis has limited cervical motion and is scheduled for general anesthesia. Which focused exam best characterizes the structures most relevant to mask ventilation and laryngoscopy?
options: Teeth, jaw space, and neck mobility
questions.explanation: The airway exam inspects dentition and the oral cavity, mouth opening and Mallampati class, the mandibular space, and cervical mobility, which rheumatoid arthritis can restrict. Nasal patency, thyroid size, and chest findings matter in specific cases but do not characterize laryngoscopy conditions.

questions.stem: A patient has acromegaly, another has a large goiter, and a third has Pierre Robin sequence. Why do these diagnoses matter during airway assessment?
options: Each can distort airway anatomy in its own way
All predict the same problem and technique
Only the goiter can affect the airway
questions.explanation: Airway difficulty can come from metabolic disease such as acromegaly, with large tongue and soft tissue, structural lesions such as a goiter compressing the trachea, and congenital anomalies such as Pierre Robin sequence, with micrognathia. Each causes a different problem, so the plan is individualized rather than mandated.

questions.stem: A patient with Parkinson disease is scheduled for surgery. Which preoperative finding is most important to establish as a neurologic baseline rather than treating it as a new postoperative complication later?
options: Prior response to a spinal anesthetic
Usual tremor and current dopaminergic drugs
Baseline visual acuity in each eye
questions.explanation: Documenting the usual tremor, rigidity, swallowing problems, and current antiparkinsonian medication schedule establishes a baseline so postoperative changes are recognized. It also guides continuing carbidopa-levodopa and avoiding dopamine antagonists such as metoclopramide and droperidol.

questions.stem: A patient with epilepsy is scheduled for surgery. Which history provides the most useful basis for perioperative seizure-risk planning?
options: Medication list by itself, since triggers do not matter
Time of the last seizure by itself
Seizure type by itself, as drugs are charted
Type, frequency, triggers, drugs, last seizure
questions.explanation: Seizure type, frequency, known triggers, current antiepileptic drugs and adherence, and the time of the last seizure together show how well controlled the epilepsy is and guide continuing medications and avoiding triggers such as hyperventilation or proconvulsant drugs. No single element is enough.

questions.stem: A patient with a remote stroke is scheduled for carotid endarterectomy. Which preoperative neurologic documentation is most useful for distinguishing a new perioperative event from an old deficit?
options: Baseline motor, sensory, and speech deficits
questions.explanation: Before carotid surgery, documenting any residual weakness, sensory loss, speech or visual deficits from the prior stroke allows a new postoperative deficit to be recognized quickly and acted on. A single element such as pupil size or reflexes misses most baseline deficits.

questions.stem: A patient reports chronic neuralgia in the operative-side extremity. Which planning consequence is most appropriate?
options: Document symptoms; protect the limb in positioning
Use inhalation induction to prevent flares
questions.explanation: Chronic neuralgia in the operative limb is documented as a baseline so postoperative symptoms can be compared, and the limb is padded and positioned carefully to avoid aggravating it. It is not an absolute contraindication to regional anesthesia, though the risks and benefits are discussed, and induction technique and blockers do not affect it.

questions.stem: Which THREE findings most increase the risk of postoperative delirium and the need for a documented cognitive baseline? (Select 3)
options: Planned regional rather than general anesthesia
questions.explanation: Preexisting cognitive impairment, a previous episode of postoperative delirium, and sensory impairment are strong predictors, so a documented baseline lets new confusion be recognized. Regional anesthesia has not been shown to lower delirium risk compared with general anesthesia, which makes it a tempting but incorrect choice. Higher education and a short outpatient procedure are associated with lower, not higher, risk.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old with hearing loss, mild dementia, and 11 home medications presents for hip repair. Which postoperative complication is most strongly suggested by this cluster of preoperative findings?
questions.explanation: Advanced age, preexisting cognitive impairment, sensory impairment such as hearing loss, and polypharmacy are classic risk factors for postoperative delirium, especially after hip fracture. Urinary retention, pressure injury, and nausea can occur but are not specifically predicted by this cluster.

questions.stem: Which two patients most clearly require a detailed neurologic baseline because postoperative findings could otherwise be difficult to interpret? (Select 2)
options: A patient for cataract surgery under topical
A patient with remote migraines for hernia repair
A patient with diabetic neuropathy before a popliteal block
A patient scheduled for carotid endarterectomy
A patient for dental extraction under MAC
questions.explanation: A detailed neurologic baseline is needed when preexisting deficits could be confused with new injury, as with neuropathy before a nerve block, or when the surgery risks neurologic injury, as with carotid endarterectomy. Remote migraine and routine procedures without neurologic risk need only a standard screening exam.

questions.stem: A patient with preexisting lower-extremity sensory loss is scheduled for regional anesthesia. Why is a detailed neurologic examination before the block especially important?
options: It records which deficits predate the block
It determines the ASA physical status
It sets the local anesthetic dose
questions.explanation: Documenting preexisting sensory loss before a block separates old deficits from any new nerve injury afterward, which guides evaluation and protects the patient and clinician. The exam does not set ASA class, the dose, or toxicity risk.

questions.stem: A patient with a recent TIA is scheduled for carotid endarterectomy. Which preoperative step most directly improves detection of a new perioperative neurologic injury?
options: Rely on the neurologist's admission note
A detailed, documented baseline neuro exam
Delay surgery a fixed six weeks
Document the airway examination by itself
questions.explanation: A detailed neurologic exam just before carotid endarterectomy, covering motor, sensory, speech, and visual function, lets the team recognize a new deficit immediately after surgery. An older admission note may not reflect the current state, and timing of carotid surgery after TIA is individualized, often within two weeks.

questions.stem: A patient is planned for MAC with local infiltration, and the surgeon expects no airway intervention. Which assessment should still be completed because the anesthetic may unexpectedly deepen or convert?
options: An airway exam if conversion is planned
No airway exam, since the surgeon decides
An airway exam if general is chosen
questions.explanation: MAC can deepen unexpectedly or need conversion to general anesthesia, so a complete airway evaluation is performed before every anesthetic, whatever the plan. The anesthesia provider, not the surgeon, is responsible for the airway.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old drinks a pint of vodka daily and takes alprazolam 2 mg at night. He needs a far larger midazolam dose than expected, then becomes apneic after one more small dose. Which history should have shaped your dosing?
questions.explanation: Chronic alcohol and benzodiazepine use creates cross-tolerance, so larger midazolam doses are needed at first, but the margin before respiratory depression narrows, and one more small dose can cause apnea. Anxiety and caffeine do not explain both effects, and OSA was not described.

questions.stem: A patient with a subdural hematoma has new confusion and needs urgent surgery. Which preinduction examination is most important for later determining whether neurologic status changed perioperatively?
options: A focused airway and spine examination
A neurologic review of the head CT
questions.explanation: New confusion with a subdural hematoma calls for a detailed bedside neurologic exam, including mental status, pupils, motor and sensory function, so any postoperative change can be judged against it. The CT shows anatomy, not function, and orientation questions alone miss focal deficits. An airway exam is needed but does not document neurologic status.

questions.stem: A thyroidectomy patient has Mallampati IV anatomy and limited cervical extension. Which preparation best addresses the anticipated difficulty before induction?
options: A standard blade with suction only
Nasal cannula oxygen as the backup
VL and difficult-airway cart at bedside
An extra IV in place of airway gear
questions.explanation: Mallampati IV with limited neck extension predicts difficult laryngoscopy, so a videolaryngoscope, bougie, supraglottic airway, and the difficult airway cart are ready before induction, with awake techniques considered. A standard blade alone, nasal oxygen, or extra IV access does not address airway rescue.

questions.stem: Which patient most needs a detailed preoperative neurologic baseline because postoperative mental-status changes would otherwise be difficult to interpret?
questions.explanation: A patient with dementia and high delirium risk needs a documented baseline mental status, because postoperative confusion is otherwise hard to tell apart from the usual state. Controlled hypertension, stable asthma, and prior PONV do not create that interpretation problem.

questions.stem: A patient has a chronic essential tremor. Which preoperative use of this finding is most important?
options: Treat it as a sign of Parkinson disease
Record it as a neurologic baseline
Treat it as a contraindication to blocks
Use it to predict postoperative delirium
questions.explanation: Essential tremor is part of the neurologic baseline, so documenting it prevents postoperative tremor from being mistaken for a new problem and alerts the team to positioning and monitoring artifact. It is distinct from Parkinson disease, does not contraindicate regional anesthesia, and does not predict delirium.

questions.stem: The MOANS mnemonic is used to predict which airway problem?
questions.explanation: MOANS predicts difficult mask ventilation: Mask seal problems such as a beard, Obesity or obstruction, Age over about 55, No teeth, and Stiff lungs or high airway resistance. LEMON predicts difficult laryngoscopy, RODS difficult supraglottic airway use, and SMART difficult cricothyrotomy.

questions.stem: A patient has recurrent migraines. Which history is most useful for distinguishing baseline symptoms from a perioperative neurologic problem?
options: The names of current migraine medications
How often attacks occur in a typical month
Whether a visual aura precedes each attack
Pattern, triggers, drugs, and last episode
questions.explanation: Knowing the usual migraine pattern, frequency, triggers, medications, and timing of the last episode lets postoperative headache be distinguished from a new problem such as post-dural puncture headache or intracranial pathology. Migraine medications such as triptans and ergots also matter for interactions.

questions.stem: A patient with cervical myelopathy is scheduled for laminectomy. Which additional preoperative examination is most important for interpreting postoperative neurologic findings?
options: A focused airway and neck examination
Neurologic review of the cervical MRI
questions.explanation: Cervical myelopathy can cause motor, sensory, and reflex deficits, so a detailed bedside neurologic exam is recorded before surgery to judge whether postoperative findings are new. The MRI shows compression but not the patient's functional deficits, and the airway exam, while needed for positioning and intubation, does not establish the neurologic baseline.

questions.stem: A patient has Mallampati II anatomy, three-fingerbreadth mouth opening, a full beard, and a short thick neck. Which conclusion best avoids false reassurance?
options: Mallampati II rules out difficult intubation
Modest findings can combine to cause difficulty
A beard affects intubation but not ventilation
questions.explanation: No single airway test is reliable, so individually modest findings such as a beard, a short thick neck, and limited mobility can together make mask ventilation or intubation difficult despite a reassuring Mallampati class. A beard mainly impairs the mask seal, which is why the full picture is integrated into the airway plan.

questions.stem: A patient previously received extensive neck radiation and now has fixed, poorly compliant anterior neck tissues despite a modest Mallampati score. What is the key implication?
options: Acquired change may outweigh the Mallampati
Radiation is irrelevant with normal mouth opening
questions.explanation: Prior neck radiation leaves fibrotic, noncompliant tissue that can make mask ventilation, laryngoscopy, and front-of-neck access difficult even with a reassuring Mallampati score. It does not mandate regional anesthesia, normal mouth opening does not cancel it, and its effects extend beyond extubation.

questions.stem: An older adult takes numerous medications, including several with deliriogenic effects. Which delirium risk factor is most amenable to preoperative modification?
questions.explanation: Polypharmacy is the delirium risk factor that can be changed before surgery, by stopping or substituting deliriogenic drugs such as anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, and some antihistamines. Advanced age and baseline cognitive impairment cannot be modified, and hearing impairment is managed with hearing aids rather than prevented.

questions.stem: A patient with Parkinson disease develops postoperative nausea. Which antiemetic should be avoided?
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide, droperidol, and prochlorperazine block central dopamine receptors and can sharply worsen parkinsonian rigidity and tremor, so they are avoided. Ondansetron and dexamethasone are safe choices, and carbidopa-levodopa should be continued on schedule.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic left-arm weakness after stroke is scheduled for a right-sided regional block. Which action best prevents a preexisting deficit from being misattributed to the anesthetic?
options: Ask about new weakness after the block wears off
Rely on the stroke diagnosis in the problem list
Examine the left arm at the end of the case
Document the baseline weakness before the block
questions.explanation: Recording the chronic left-arm weakness before the block ensures it is not later mistaken for a block or positioning injury. Asking after the block or examining at the end of the case has no documented baseline to compare against, and a problem-list diagnosis does not describe the actual strength deficit.

questions.stem: An older adult uses hearing aids and has significant visual impairment. Why should these devices and deficits matter to the perioperative plan?
questions.explanation: Hearing and vision impairment make reorientation harder after surgery and are established delirium risk factors, so hearing aids and glasses should be available as early as possible in recovery. They do not predict difficult airways, dictate the anesthetic type, or change local anesthetic dosing.

questions.stem: During the airway exam, a patient cannot bring the lower incisors up to cover any of the upper lip. What does this finding predict?
questions.explanation: The upper lip bite test assesses mandibular protrusion; class III, inability to reach the upper lip at all, predicts difficult laryngoscopy because the jaw cannot move forward to make room for the tongue. It complements Mallampati class and thyromental distance and does not assess mask ventilation directly.

questions.stem: A 70-kg patient's resting oxygen consumption is about 245 mL/min. During an activity it rises to roughly 1,000 mL/min. Approximately what functional capacity does this represent?
questions.explanation: One MET is about 3.5 mL/kg/min of oxygen, which for 70 kg is 3.5 ÃÂÃÂ 70 = 245 mL/min. An activity using 1,000 mL/min is 1,000 ÃÂÃÂ· 245, or about 4 METs, roughly climbing a flight of stairs. Choosing 1 or 2 METs underestimates the ratio, and 10 METs would need about 2,450 mL/min.

questions.stem: A patient walks two miles and performs yard work without chest pain or dyspnea. Which inference about functional capacity is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Walking two miles and doing yard work without symptoms corresponds to more than 4 METs, which indicates adequate cardiopulmonary reserve and usually means further cardiac testing will not change management if there is no active cardiac condition. Formal testing is not needed to estimate capacity from history.

questions.stem: Which Duke Activity Status Index (DASI) score most closely corresponds to the commonly used 4-MET threshold?
questions.explanation: The DASI is a structured questionnaire about daily activities, and a score above about 34 corresponds to roughly 4 METs, so it gives a more standardized estimate of functional capacity than a simple stair question. Lower scores suggest limited capacity and may prompt further risk assessment.

questions.stem: Which activity history most strongly reassures you that a patient can achieve at least moderate functional capacity without symptoms?
options: Scrubbing floors or moving heavy furniture
Walking slowly from room to room
questions.explanation: Heavy housework such as scrubbing floors or moving furniture requires about 4 or more METs, so doing it without symptoms shows at least moderate functional capacity. Dressing, eating, and slow walking at home are 1 to 2 MET activities and say little about reserve.

questions.stem: A patient can perform basic activities of daily living but must stop halfway up one flight of stairs because of dyspnea. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: At least 4 METs since the patient lives independently
Normal for age and adds no information
Below 4 METs; further assessment may be needed
The dyspnea proves a pulmonary cause
questions.explanation: Stopping halfway up one flight because of dyspnea means functional capacity below about 4 METs, so in a patient facing elevated-risk surgery, further cardiac risk assessment such as biomarkers or testing may be appropriate. Independence in basic activities requires fewer than 4 METs, and dyspnea can be cardiac or pulmonary.

questions.stem: A patient reports activities corresponding to about 5 METs but has never undergone exercise testing. How should the recorded value be interpreted?
options: An objective measure equal to CPET results
A value derived from ejection fraction
A history-based estimate dependent on the report
questions.explanation: METs estimated from activity history are subjective and depend on how accurately the patient reports what they can do, so they can over- or underestimate capacity. Objective values come from exercise testing or cardiopulmonary exercise testing, and ejection fraction does not determine METs.

questions.stem: A patient's severe osteoarthritis and lower extremity joint pain make self-reported activity history (functional capacity) unreliable before an elevated-risk noncardiac surgery. Which test can objectively quantify functional capacity when such measurement would change management?
options: CPET (Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing) or another suitable exercise test
questions.explanation: Severe arthritis or musculoskeletal limitations prevent patients from achieving or reporting normal physical exertion (such as climbing stairs), rendering functional capacity assessment unreliable. According to ACC/AHA perioperative guidelines, when functional capacity is unknown or limited by non-cardiac conditions and results will change management, objective measurement via cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) or pharmacologic stress imaging is indicated. Resting tests (ECG, echo, chest X-ray) do not measure functional capacity.

questions.stem: On cardiopulmonary exercise testing before major abdominal surgery, which finding identifies a patient at high risk of perioperative complications?
options: Peak heart rate above 85% of predicted
questions.explanation: An anaerobic threshold below about 11 mL/kg/min, or a low peak VO2, marks limited cardiopulmonary reserve and is associated with higher morbidity and mortality after major surgery, so it can guide prehabilitation, postoperative level of care, or surgical decisions. High thresholds and peak VO2 indicate good reserve.

questions.stem: Which two activities most strongly support functional capacity of at least 4 METs? (Select 2)
options: Walking one block on level ground
questions.explanation: Singles tennis and walking up a hill require at least 4 METs, which indicates adequate functional capacity for most noncardiac surgery. Walking one block on level ground, desk work, washing dishes, and slow walking require only 1 to 3 METs and do not show adequate reserve.

questions.stem: An older adult cannot relate to stair-climbing questions. Which alternative history best estimates functional capacity using familiar daily activities?
options: Number of hours slept on a typical night
Ability to dress and bathe without help
Shopping, walking between stores, or mowing
Number of chronic medications taken daily
questions.explanation: Familiar activities such as shopping with walking between stores, pushing a lawn mower, or carrying groceries give a practical MET estimate when stair questions do not apply. Dressing and bathing require only 1 to 2 METs, and sleep or medication counts do not measure exertional capacity.

questions.stem: In an older patient with limited functional capacity before major noncardiac surgery, which blood test can help refine perioperative cardiac risk?
questions.explanation: Elevated preoperative NT-proBNP or BNP independently predicts perioperative cardiac events and can refine risk in older patients with limited capacity before major surgery. CRP and D-dimer are nonspecific, and HbA1c reflects glucose control rather than cardiac risk.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetes and hypertension cannot walk far because of severe knee arthritis and is scheduled for an elevated-risk procedure. How should the limitation be interpreted?
options: Orthopedic limitation makes functional capacity irrelevant to perioperative assessment
Functional capacity should be assumed above 4 METs because the limitation is orthopedic
Functional capacity should be assumed below 4 METs and stress testing ordered automatically
Functional capacity is uncertain, so further risk assessment may be needed
questions.explanation: When arthritis limits walking, history cannot show whether the heart could handle 4 METs, so functional capacity is treated as unknown rather than assumed good or poor. With diabetes, hypertension, and an elevated-risk procedure, guidelines support further assessment, such as biomarkers or testing when the result would change management, rather than automatic stress testing.

questions.stem: A patient can climb stairs briskly but developed new chest pain at rest last week. Which finding should drive the preoperative decision?
options: The stair climbing, showing adequate reserve
The MET estimate, which excludes unstable disease
The new angina, an active cardiac problem
The ASA status, which outranks symptoms
questions.explanation: New chest pain at rest is unstable angina, an active cardiac condition that requires evaluation before elective surgery regardless of good exercise tolerance. Functional capacity guides testing only when there is no active condition, and ASA status does not override symptoms.

questions.stem: Which finding is an active cardiac condition that warrants evaluation and treatment before elective noncardiac surgery?
questions.explanation: Active cardiac conditions, including decompensated heart failure, unstable or severe angina, significant arrhythmias, and severe symptomatic valvular disease, warrant evaluation and treatment before elective surgery. A remote MI, controlled hypertension, and an asymptomatic bundle branch block are risk factors or incidental findings, not active conditions.

questions.stem: A patient is ASA III with an RCRI of 1 and functional capacity around 5 METs. How should these measures be interpreted?
options: Together, since each covers a different aspect
METs by themselves decide whether to proceed
RCRI by itself decides whether to proceed
ASA status by itself decides whether to proceed
questions.explanation: ASA status describes overall systemic disease, RCRI estimates major cardiac complication risk, and METs reflect functional reserve, so they are interpreted together with the surgery's risk rather than any one deciding alone. This patient has moderate disease, one cardiac risk factor, and adequate capacity.

questions.stem: A patient has functional capacity below 4 METs before an elevated-risk procedure. What does that threshold imply?
options: Choose regional anesthesia instead of further assessment
Proceed because procedural risk is the only factor that matters
Proceed automatically if the RCRI is zero
Further guideline-based cardiac risk assessment may be appropriate
questions.explanation: Functional capacity below 4 METs, or unknown capacity, before an elevated-risk procedure means the patient's cardiac reserve is unproven, so guideline-based assessment such as biomarkers, testing, or consultation may be appropriate when it would change management. An RCRI of zero would place the patient at low risk, and choosing regional anesthesia does not replace the assessment.

questions.stem: A patient swims laps and performs heavy housework without chest pain or dyspnea. How should this history influence preoperative cardiac assessment?
options: It proves coronary artery disease is absent
Moderate capacity; symptoms and surgery still matter
It mandates CPET since the activities are strenuous
It removes the need to ask about new symptoms
questions.explanation: Swimming laps and heavy housework without symptoms show at least 4 METs, which supports adequate reserve, but active cardiac symptoms and the risk of the procedure still take precedence. Good capacity does not exclude coronary disease, and it reduces rather than increases the need for testing.

questions.stem: A patient says he 'walks a lot,' but collateral history reveals dyspnea after half a block. Which limitation of history-based MET estimation does this illustrate?
options: It is an objective value derived from echocardiography
It is subjective and depends on the accuracy of reported activity
It is validated only in pediatric patients
It predicts pulmonary complications but not cardiovascular risk
questions.explanation: METs estimated from history depend on the patient's report, so they can be overestimated, as when a patient says he walks a lot but becomes dyspneic after half a block. Objective tools such as cardiopulmonary exercise testing are more reliable. History-based METs are used in adults and help predict cardiovascular risk.

questions.stem: Which history most strongly suggests functional capacity below the commonly used 4-MET threshold?
options: Climbing one flight slowly without symptoms
Stopping on one flight of stairs from dyspnea
questions.explanation: Needing to stop during a single flight of stairs because of dyspnea indicates capacity below about 4 METs. Scrubbing floors and walking uphill without symptoms are 4 MET or greater activities, and climbing a flight slowly without symptoms suggests capacity near the threshold.

questions.stem: Which finding is one of the six Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) risk factors?
questions.explanation: The RCRI factors are high-risk surgery, ischemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated diabetes, and creatinine above 2 mg/dL, with each adding risk of major cardiac complications. Age, hypertension, and atrial fibrillation matter but are not RCRI factors.

questions.stem: A patient had a drug-eluting coronary stent placed 4 months ago for chronic coronary disease and now requests elective noncardiac surgery that would require interruption of an antiplatelet agent. Which plan best reflects current perioperative guidance?
options: Delay; about 6 months after DES is preferred
Proceed, since every DES is safe after 3 months
Proceed after stopping all antiplatelets 7 days
Delay all surgery 12 months after any DES
questions.explanation: After a drug-eluting stent for chronic coronary disease, delaying elective noncardiac surgery that requires interrupting antiplatelet therapy for about 6 months is generally preferred; time-sensitive surgery may be considered after 3 months when delay is harmful. Stopping all antiplatelets early risks stent thrombosis, and 12 months applies after acute coronary syndromes.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient had a bare-metal coronary stent placed 5 weeks ago and now requests elective hernia repair that would require interruption of antiplatelet therapy. Which concern is most important?
options: Past 30 days, surgery is automatically fine
Recent stent makes stopping antiplatelets risky
Any bare-metal stent needs a 12-month delay
Antiplatelets can stop safely after 7 days
questions.explanation: Five weeks after a bare-metal stent, interrupting antiplatelet therapy for elective surgery still carries stent thrombosis risk, so timing and antiplatelet management are planned individually with cardiology, often delaying to at least 30 days and preferably longer while continuing aspirin. A fixed day count alone is not enough.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient had a myocardial infarction 5 weeks ago that was managed medically without revascularization and now requests elective surgery. Which principle is most appropriate?
options: Use the same timing as uncomplicated CABG
Delay the case and reassess risk
questions.explanation: A myocardial infarction 5 weeks ago, managed medically, substantially raises perioperative cardiac risk, so elective surgery is postponed, commonly to at least 60 days, and ischemic risk reassessed rather than relying on a single cutoff or functional capacity. Timing after revascularization follows different considerations.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient underwent CABG 4 months ago, has recovered without recurrent ischemic symptoms, and requests elective shoulder replacement. How should the prior CABG affect timing?
options: Proceed automatically once 60 days have passed
Elective surgery is barred for 6 months after CABG
Proceed automatically once 30 days have passed
questions.explanation: Timing after CABG depends on the patient's recovery, symptoms, surgical risk, and need for further evaluation rather than a fixed waiting period. A well-recovered patient without ischemic symptoms may be ready, while a symptomatic one needs evaluation regardless of elapsed time.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Surgery for a patient with a drug-eluting stent placed 3 months ago cannot be delayed. Which antiplatelet approach is generally recommended?
options: Stop aspirin and clopidogrel 10 days before
Replace both drugs with heparin bridging
Continue aspirin through surgery if possible
questions.explanation: When surgery cannot wait after a recent stent, aspirin is continued perioperatively whenever the bleeding risk allows, and the P2Y12 inhibitor is stopped for the shortest safe period and restarted as soon as possible, coordinated with cardiology. Heparin does not protect against stent thrombosis, and stopping both drugs raises that risk.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient develops perioperative myocardial injury during profound anemia and hypotension without evidence of acute plaque rupture. Which mechanism best explains the event?
options: Acute coronary plaque rupture with thrombosis
Sudden cardiac death without biomarker evidence
questions.explanation: Myocardial injury during severe anemia and hypotension without plaque rupture is a type 2 MI, caused by oxygen supply falling below demand. Treatment corrects the cause, such as transfusing and restoring pressure, rather than PCI. Plaque rupture with thrombosis defines a type 1 MI, and PCI-related injury is type 4.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Which THREE findings increase this vascular-surgery patient's probability of coronary artery disease? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Smoking, diabetes, and peripheral vascular disease are major risk factors, and atherosclerosis in one vascular bed strongly predicts it in the coronaries. Treated hypothyroidism is not an independent risk factor, and a normal BMI and a cholesterol of 160 mg/dL point toward lower rather than higher risk.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: One patient has unchanged exertional angina for three years; another developed new rest angina twice this week. Which preoperative distinction matters most?
options: Both may proceed since both have known angina already
Both need identical cardiac evaluation before surgery
New rest angina may proceed; stable angina needs workup
Stable angina may proceed; new rest angina needs workup
questions.explanation: Angina that has been stable for years is a risk factor managed within the overall assessment, while new angina at rest is unstable and an active cardiac condition requiring evaluation before elective surgery. Treating both the same either overtests the stable patient or misses the unstable one.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient with poor functional capacity has an abnormal noninvasive ischemia study before major vascular surgery, and the result will change management. Which test can directly define coronary anatomy when further invasive evaluation is indicated?
questions.explanation: Coronary angiography directly shows the location and severity of coronary stenoses, so it is the test used when an abnormal stress study and the clinical picture justify invasive evaluation. Echocardiography assesses function and valves, while ECG and Holter monitoring detect rhythm and ischemic changes without defining anatomy.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient requires ischemia evaluation but cannot exercise because of severe arthritis. Which testing strategy best preserves the purpose of stress testing?
options: Treadmill stress at a very low workload
questions.explanation: When a patient cannot exercise adequately, dobutamine stress echocardiography or vasodilator nuclear imaging provokes ischemia pharmacologically. A very low treadmill workload never reaches the heart-rate target needed to unmask ischemia, Holter monitoring records rhythm, and tilt-table testing evaluates syncope.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient with known CAD says a cardiologist evaluated him last month. Which next step yields the most actionable perioperative information?
options: Repeat a stress test before surgery
Ask whether the patient takes a statin
questions.explanation: A recent cardiology evaluation contains test results, current risk assessment, and specific perioperative recommendations, so obtaining it is the most useful next step. Repeating testing duplicates work without new indications, and a statin question gives only one piece of information.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient with hypertension takes lisinopril daily and is scheduled for a long abdominal operation with expected blood loss. Which perioperative concern most often guides holding the morning dose?
options: Hyperkalemia from a single missed dose
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors and ARBs blunt the renin-angiotensin response, so after induction and with blood loss they can cause hypotension that responds poorly to usual vasopressors; many clinicians hold them about 24 hours before major surgery. Unlike clonidine or beta-blockers, stopping them briefly does not cause significant rebound.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Repeated preoperative blood pressures average 148/94 mmHg without acute symptoms. Which classification describes the pressure itself?
questions.explanation: Using the ACC/AHA categories, stage 2 hypertension is a systolic pressure of 140 or more or a diastolic pressure of 90 or more, so 148/94 qualifies. Stage 1 is 130 to 139 or 80 to 89, elevated is 120 to 129 with diastolic below 80, and a crisis exceeds 180/120.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient presents for elective surgery with BP 162/98 mmHg, no symptoms, and no evidence of end-organ injury. Which interpretation is most consistent with current guidance?
options: Stage 2 hypertension mandates a cardiology consult
Below 180/110 is not an independent risk factor
Systolic pressure over 160 requires a beta-blocker bolus
questions.explanation: Blood pressure below 180/110 mmHg in an asymptomatic patient without end-organ injury is not an independent predictor of perioperative cardiac complications, so elective surgery usually proceeds with follow-up arranged. Cancellation, routine consults, or a preoperative beta-blocker bolus are not required at this level.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient presents with BP 168/98 mmHg before surgery. Which three findings most directly determine whether this represents uncomplicated chronic hypertension or a higher-risk perioperative problem? (Select 3)
options: Symptoms such as syncope or dizziness
The patient's anxiety level in preop
Whether a larger cuff was used
Antihypertensive medications, doses, and last dose time
questions.explanation: Assessing preoperative hypertension focuses on end-organ dysfunction, symptoms such as syncope or chest pain, and the medication list with last-dose timing. Anxiety, cuff size, and caffeine can raise a single reading, which is why the reading is repeated, but they do not determine whether the patient faces higher perioperative risk.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient took lisinopril, amlodipine, metoprolol, and chlorthalidone on the morning of surgery. Why is the exact medication list and timing clinically important before induction?
options: It sets the dose of reversal agents
questions.explanation: Several antihypertensives taken the same morning, especially an ACE inhibitor with a diuretic and a beta-blocker, can cause marked hypotension and blunted compensation at induction, so knowing them guides induction dosing and vasopressor readiness. They do not determine reversal dosing, delirium risk, or PONV prophylaxis.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient had a drug-eluting coronary stent 8 months ago and takes aspirin alone. What is the most important preoperative issue before deciding whether aspirin should be interrupted?
options: Restart dual antiplatelet therapy for surgery
Weigh bleeding risk against thrombotic risk
Stop aspirin since six months have passed
Delay surgery until 12 months after DES
questions.explanation: Eight months after a drug-eluting stent on aspirin alone, aspirin is usually continued perioperatively because stopping it raises coronary thrombotic risk, unless the procedure carries prohibitive bleeding risk such as some intracranial or spinal surgery. The decision weighs both risks with the surgeon and cardiologist.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient with remote myocardial infarction presents for colectomy. Which cardiac-assessment goal is most useful for building the anesthetic plan?
options: Avoid elective surgery after any previous MI
Diagnose every coronary lesion before surgery
Define baseline, active disease, risk, and monitoring
Obtain cardiology clearance for any history of CAD
questions.explanation: The goal of preoperative cardiac assessment is to establish baseline function, find active cardiac conditions, estimate risk, and plan monitoring and optimization. A remote MI does not bar surgery, exhaustive testing rarely changes outcomes, and clearance is not a substitute for the anesthesia team's own risk assessment.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Which four findings should interrupt routine elective-surgery planning until further cardiac evaluation is considered? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Decompensated heart failure, unstable angina, recent myocardial infarction, and unexplained syncope are active cardiac conditions that interrupt elective planning for evaluation and treatment, as are significant arrhythmias and severe symptomatic valve disease. Remote PCI without symptoms and stable rate-controlled atrial fibrillation can usually proceed.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Four patients with similar coronary disease are scheduled for different procedures. Which operation contributes the greatest additional cardiac stress from procedural risk?
options: Superficial skin excision under local anesthesia
questions.explanation: Open aortic aneurysm repair is high-risk surgery with large fluid shifts, aortic clamping, and major hemodynamic stress. Cataract surgery, skin excision, and carpal tunnel release are low-risk procedures with minimal cardiac stress. Procedure risk and patient risk combine to define perioperative cardiac risk.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient with CAD and poor functional capacity is scheduled for one of four procedures. Which operation adds the least procedural cardiac risk?
questions.explanation: Cataract extraction is a low-risk procedure with minimal fluid shifts or hemodynamic stress, so it adds the least procedural cardiac risk even in a patient with CAD. Aortic aneurysm repair, esophagectomy, and open colectomy are elevated-risk operations with major fluid shifts and stress responses.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A cardiology note from two years ago describes stable disease, but the patient now reports worsening exertional dyspnea. Which information should drive today's decision?
options: The option of regional instead of evaluation
The old cardiology note in the chart
A normal resting ECG from this morning
questions.explanation: Worsening exertional dyspnea is a new symptom that may represent progressing ischemia or heart failure, so it warrants updated cardiac evaluation before elective surgery. A two-year-old note does not reflect the current state, a normal resting ECG does not exclude disease, and choosing regional anesthesia does not remove the risk.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient with prior MI takes amiodarone. Which ECG review is most complete for identifying findings that could alter the anesthetic plan?
options: Rhythm, conduction, infarct, ischemia, and QT
P waves and QRS width, with QT ignored
Axis and voltage, as rhythm is monitored later
Rate and rhythm, as ischemia needs an echo
questions.explanation: A complete preoperative ECG review covers rhythm, conduction blocks, prior infarct patterns, ischemic changes, and the QT interval, which matters with amiodarone because added QT-prolonging drugs such as ondansetron or droperidol can raise torsades risk. Reviewing only part of the tracing can miss findings that change the plan.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: An asymptomatic patient's blood pressure is 186/114 mmHg on repeated readings before elective knee replacement. Which approach is generally recommended?
options: Proceed after IV labetalol lowers the pressure
Delay surgery to improve blood pressure control
Proceed since the patient has no symptoms
Proceed under spinal to avoid laryngoscopy
questions.explanation: Sustained pressures of 180/110 mmHg or higher are commonly treated as a reason to postpone elective surgery and optimize control over days to weeks, because these patients have more lability, ischemia, and arrhythmias. Rapidly lowering pressure in preop does not correct the underlying risk, and neuraxial anesthesia can cause marked hypotension.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient takes metoprolol daily for stable coronary disease and is scheduled for hip arthroplasty. What is the recommended perioperative beta-blocker plan?
options: Hold metoprolol for 48 hours before surgery
Switch to high-dose metoprolol the morning of surgery
Continue metoprolol, including the morning dose
Hold metoprolol and give IV esmolol instead
questions.explanation: Patients already on beta-blockers should continue them perioperatively, because abrupt withdrawal can cause rebound tachycardia, hypertension, and ischemia. Starting high-dose beta-blockade on the day of surgery, as in the POISE trial, increased stroke and mortality, so new therapy is not begun just before surgery.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Which preoperative profile most strongly supports proceeding to an intermediate-risk operation without additional cardiac testing?
options: Tachycardia with an S3 and crackles
Bradycardia with a gallop and edema
Normal exam, controlled BP, over 4 METs
questions.explanation: A normal cardiovascular exam with regular rhythm and no JVD, controlled blood pressure, and functional capacity above 4 METs mean no active cardiac condition and adequate reserve, so additional testing is unlikely to change management for intermediate-risk surgery. The other profiles suggest heart failure or valvular disease that needs evaluation.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient takes atorvastatin for coronary disease and is scheduled for vascular surgery. What is the recommended perioperative statin plan?
