options: Hold the statin 1 week before surgery
Hold the statin on the day of surgery
Stop the statin until the patient is eating
questions.explanation: Statins should be continued perioperatively in patients already taking them, and starting one is reasonable before vascular surgery, because they are associated with fewer cardiac events. Their benefit likely includes plaque stabilization and anti-inflammatory effects, and withdrawal may increase cardiac risk.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Which two physical findings most strongly suggest volume-overloaded heart failure during preoperative assessment? (Select 2)
options: An S4 gallop with clear lungs
questions.explanation: Jugular venous distension and pulmonary crackles reflect elevated filling pressures and congestion from volume-overloaded heart failure, along with edema and an S3. Wheezing suggests bronchospasm, an S4 reflects a stiff ventricle without necessarily overload, and cyanosis and bradycardia are nonspecific.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient had an MI treated with PCI 2 months ago and now needs noncardiac surgery. Which missing detail is most important for judging stent and antiplatelet risk?
options: Stent type, indication, and DAPT plan
Peak troponin level during the MI
Length of the PCI hospital stay
questions.explanation: Stent thrombosis risk depends on the stent type, why it was placed (acute coronary syndrome versus stable disease), and how long dual antiplatelet therapy is required, which together decide whether surgery can proceed and whether antiplatelets can be interrupted. Infarct location, peak troponin, and hospital stay do not answer that question.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Two patients both have BP 168/98 mmHg. One is asymptomatic; the other has headache, blurred vision, and new proteinuria. Why should the second patient be treated differently in the risk assessment?
options: The asymptomatic patient has greater perioperative risk
Identical pressures imply identical risk in both patients
End-organ symptoms matter once pressure reaches 200/120
These findings suggest acute end-organ injury
questions.explanation: Headache, blurred vision, and new proteinuria at the same pressure suggest acute end-organ involvement, which raises perioperative risk and usually warrants delaying elective surgery for evaluation and control. Asymptomatic pressures below 180/110 mmHg without end-organ injury do not independently predict cardiovascular complications.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient with long-standing hypertension has a preoperative pressure of 154/92 mmHg but no acute symptoms. Why does the history still matter even if this single value does not mandate cancellation?
options: It may reflect target-organ disease and reserve
It calls for a beta-blocker load
questions.explanation: Long-standing hypertension can cause left ventricular hypertrophy, renal disease, and cerebrovascular disease, and it shifts autoregulation, so the history shapes blood pressure targets and reserve even when one reading is acceptable. It does not by itself require an arterial line, a beta-blocker load, or cancellation.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Repeated preoperative blood pressures average 134/86 mmHg. Which category best matches those values?
questions.explanation: Stage 1 hypertension is a systolic pressure of 130 to 139 or a diastolic pressure of 80 to 89 mmHg, so 134/86 fits this category. Elevated blood pressure is 120 to 129 systolic with a diastolic under 80, and stage 2 begins at 140 or 90.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Four patients with valve disease are scheduled for elective noncardiac surgery. Which lesion creates the greatest concern for perioperative hemodynamic collapse?
questions.explanation: Severe aortic stenosis, with a valve area under 1 cmÃÂÃÂ², carries the greatest risk of perioperative hemodynamic collapse because the fixed obstruction limits cardiac output and the hypertrophied ventricle depends on coronary perfusion pressure. Mild MR, moderate AR, and mitral valve prolapse are generally well tolerated.

questions.stem: An echocardiogram shows aortic valve area 0.8 cmÃÂÃÂ², mean gradient 44 mmHg, and peak velocity 4.2 m/s. Which interpretation best connects the measurements to perioperative risk?
options: The findings represent moderate aortic stenosis with low perioperative risk
The findings meet severe aortic stenosis criteria and indicate high perioperative risk
The findings represent mild aortic stenosis with no special precautions
The findings show aortic sclerosis without stenosis
questions.explanation: A valve area under 1.0 cmÃÂÃÂ², a mean gradient of 40 mmHg or more, and a peak velocity of 4 m/s or more each meet criteria for severe aortic stenosis. Severe AS carries a high risk of hypotension, ischemia, and sudden death under anesthesia, so it usually prompts cardiology review before elective surgery.

questions.stem: A patient with severe mitral stenosis is scheduled for surgery. Which hemodynamic change is most likely to precipitate pulmonary edema?
options: A modest rise in systemic resistance
questions.explanation: In mitral stenosis, left ventricular filling depends on time in diastole across the narrowed valve, so tachycardia raises left atrial pressure and can cause pulmonary edema; new atrial fibrillation is especially poorly tolerated. Goals include a slow-normal heart rate, maintained sinus rhythm, careful fluids, and avoiding hypoxia or hypercarbia that raise pulmonary pressures.

questions.stem: An echocardiogram shows aortic jet velocity 3.4 m/s, mean gradient 28 mmHg, and valve area 1.2 cmÃÂÃÂ². Which severity category is most consistent across all three measurements?
questions.explanation: Moderate aortic stenosis is defined by a jet velocity of 3.0 to 3.9 m/s, a mean gradient of 20 to 39 mmHg, and a valve area of 1.0 to 1.5 cmÃÂÃÂ², so all three values agree here. Severe AS requires a velocity of 4 m/s or more, a gradient of 40 mmHg or more, or an area under 1.0 cmÃÂÃÂ².

questions.stem: A patient with severe aortic stenosis is scheduled for major surgery. Which physiologic problem makes abrupt anesthetic-induced hypotension especially dangerous?
options: Fixed outflow limits output and coronary flow
The ventricle readily raises stroke volume
questions.explanation: In severe aortic stenosis, the fixed outflow obstruction prevents cardiac output from rising when pressure falls, and the hypertrophied ventricle depends on diastolic pressure for coronary perfusion, so hypotension can cause ischemia and collapse. Tachycardia shortens diastole and worsens perfusion.

questions.stem: A patient with known valvular disease presents for elective hip replacement. Which information most directly defines the lesion's current severity and physiologic significance?
questions.explanation: The current severity of a valve lesion is defined by symptoms together with echocardiography, which measures gradients, valve area, and ventricular function. Murmur intensity, ECG, BNP, and functional capacity add supporting information but cannot define severity on their own.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old with exertional dyspnea has a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border. Which lesion best fits both the timing and location?
questions.explanation: A harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border in an older adult with exertional dyspnea is classic for aortic stenosis. Mitral regurgitation and aortic stenosis are systolic murmurs, while mitral stenosis and aortic regurgitation are diastolic, and tricuspid stenosis is a rare diastolic murmur at the left lower sternal border.

questions.stem: A holosystolic murmur is loudest at the apex and radiates toward the axilla. Which lesion is most likely?
questions.explanation: Mitral regurgitation produces a blowing holosystolic murmur loudest at the apex that radiates to the axilla. Aortic stenosis is a crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids, while mitral stenosis and aortic regurgitation are diastolic murmurs.

questions.stem: A young woman has a midsystolic click followed by a late systolic murmur at the apex, and the click occurs earlier when she stands. Which lesion is most likely?
questions.explanation: Mitral valve prolapse produces a midsystolic click followed by a late systolic murmur, and standing or Valsalva reduces ventricular volume so the click and murmur occur earlier. Aortic stenosis lacks a click and radiates to the carotids, while mitral stenosis and aortic regurgitation are diastolic murmurs.

questions.stem: A low-pitched middiastolic rumble with an opening snap is heard at the apex. Which lesion is most likely?
questions.explanation: Mitral stenosis produces an opening snap followed by a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble heard best at the apex. Aortic regurgitation causes a high-pitched early diastolic murmur, while mitral regurgitation and aortic stenosis are systolic murmurs.

questions.stem: A systolic murmur becomes louder with standing or Valsalva and softer with squatting. Which lesion is most consistent with this preload-sensitive pattern?
questions.explanation: Standing and Valsalva reduce preload, bringing the septum and mitral leaflet closer and worsening outflow obstruction, so the murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy grows louder, and squatting softens it. Aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation, and VSD murmurs all get softer with reduced preload, which is the opposite pattern.

questions.stem: A patient has clinical heart failure but an ejection fraction of 58%. Which classification best describes the ventricular phenotype?
options: Normal cardiac function with no heart failure
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
Heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
questions.explanation: Heart failure with an ejection fraction above about 50% is classified as heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Symptoms come mainly from impaired diastolic filling and stiffness rather than poor systolic ejection. HFrEF describes a reduced EF.

questions.stem: Two patients with heart failure face the same operation; one has EF 58% and the other EF 32%. Which feature most strongly identifies the higher-risk patient?
options: Reduced EF of 32% consistent with HFrEF
Preserved EF of 58% consistent with HFpEF
The risks are equivalent because both have heart failure
Ejection fraction does not influence perioperative risk
questions.explanation: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, such as an EF of 32%, carries higher perioperative mortality and morbidity than heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, though HFpEF still adds risk. EF guides choices about induction drugs, invasive monitoring, and fluid management.

questions.stem: Which four findings most strongly support decompensated left-ventricular dysfunction before surgery? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Orthopnea, pulmonary crackles, jugular venous distension, and resting tachycardia with tachypnea indicate elevated filling pressures and congestion from decompensated left ventricular dysfunction. An S4 reflects reduced compliance without proving decompensation, and wheezing points to bronchospasm, though cardiac asthma can mimic it.

questions.stem: A patient has insulin-treated diabetes, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, and a prior myocardial infarction and is scheduled for total knee arthroplasty. What is the classic RCRI score?
questions.explanation: Insulin-treated diabetes, creatinine above 2.0 mg/dL, and ischemic heart disease each add 1 point, for a score of 3. Knee arthroplasty is not intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, or suprainguinal vascular surgery, so it does not add the high-risk surgery point.

questions.stem: A patient has creatinine 2.3 mg/dL before elevated-risk noncardiac surgery. How does this affect the classic RCRI?
options: It counts only if dialysis is required
It does not count unless creatinine exceeds 3.0 mg/dL
questions.explanation: The classic RCRI renal criterion is a preoperative creatinine above 2.0 mg/dL, so 2.3 mg/dL adds 1 point. Dialysis is not required, and no single RCRI factor adds more than 1 point.

questions.stem: Two patients with diabetes undergo the same operation. One uses metformin only; the other requires basal-bolus insulin. Which difference changes the classic RCRI?
options: Both patients receive the same diabetes point
Insulin adds the point; metformin does not
Only metformin therapy adds the criterion
questions.explanation: The classic RCRI counts diabetes only when it requires insulin, as a marker of more advanced disease, so the basal-bolus patient gets 1 point and the metformin patient none. HbA1c is not part of the index.

questions.stem: A patient uses insulin, has prior stroke, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, and is scheduled for open AAA repair. What is the RCRI score?
questions.explanation: Insulin-treated diabetes, cerebrovascular disease, creatinine above 2.0 mg/dL, and open aortic aneurysm repair as high-risk suprainguinal vascular surgery each add 1 point, giving an RCRI of 4. Three or more points corresponds to a substantially higher risk of major cardiac complications.

questions.stem: A patient's classic RCRI score is 3. How should the score be used?
options: As a precise probability that replaces judgment
As a reason to cancel surgery automatically
As a tool that already includes frailty and METs
As one estimate integrated with other factors
questions.explanation: An RCRI of 3 or more indicates elevated risk of major cardiac complications, but the score is a population estimate that does not include functional capacity, frailty, or procedure details. It is combined with symptoms, METs, and surgical risk to decide on testing, monitoring, and optimization rather than cancelling surgery automatically.

questions.stem: A patient with no other classic RCRI risk factors is scheduled for open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair. How does the procedure affect the score?
options: The high-risk surgery criterion adds 1 point
No points, since only patient diseases count
questions.explanation: Open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair is suprainguinal vascular surgery, which meets the classic RCRI high-risk surgery criterion and adds 1 point. Each of the six RCRI factors contributes 1 point, and procedure risk is included alongside patient conditions.

questions.stem: Which THREE operations are examples of procedures that may satisfy the classic RCRI high-risk-surgery category? (Select 3)
options: Major intrathoracic surgery such as pneumonectomy
questions.explanation: The original RCRI gives a point for intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, or suprainguinal vascular surgery, so open aortic aneurysm repair, pneumonectomy, and other suprainguinal vascular operations qualify. Below-knee amputation is infrainguinal, and TURP and hip arthroplasty are not in the high-risk category even though they carry their own risks.

questions.stem: A patient with ischemic heart disease and prior heart failure is scheduled for open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair. What classic RCRI score results from those three findings?
questions.explanation: The RCRI gives one point each for ischemic heart disease, heart failure, high-risk surgery (intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, or suprainguinal vascular), cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated diabetes, and creatinine above 2 mg/dL. Open AAA repair is suprainguinal vascular surgery, so 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. Leaving out the surgical point gives 2.

questions.stem: A patient has RCRI 0, poor stair-climbing tolerance from dyspnea, and ASA III status. Why is it unsafe to stop the assessment at the RCRI score?
options: RCRI predicts pulmonary rather than cardiac events
RCRI omits capacity and overall disease burden
RCRI applies only to cardiac surgical patients
RCRI already contains METs and ASA status
questions.explanation: The RCRI estimates cardiac risk from a short list of factors and does not include functional capacity or overall disease burden. A patient with RCRI 0 but poor exercise tolerance and ASA III status may still have meaningful perioperative risk, so the score is one input, not the full assessment.

questions.stem: A patient has a prior episode of pulmonary edema and now has an S3 with jugular venous distension. Which RCRI criterion is satisfied?
questions.explanation: A history of pulmonary edema, or signs such as an S3 gallop and jugular venous distension, satisfies the RCRI congestive heart failure criterion and adds 1 point. Active signs also mean the heart failure may be decompensated, which warrants optimization before elective surgery.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic severe aortic regurgitation is scheduled for surgery. Which heart rate goal best limits regurgitant volume?
options: A normal to slightly elevated heart rate
A heart rate kept as low as tolerated
questions.explanation: In aortic regurgitation, a faster heart rate shortens diastole and reduces regurgitant time, so a normal to slightly high rate around 80 to 100/min is preferred, along with lower afterload to favor forward flow. Bradycardia lengthens diastole and worsens regurgitation and ventricular distension, and sudden increases in resistance increase regurgitant volume.

questions.stem: A blowing holodiastolic murmur is heard along the left sternal border in a patient with wide pulse pressure. Which lesion is most likely?
questions.explanation: Aortic regurgitation produces a blowing, high-pitched early or holodiastolic murmur along the left sternal border, and the large stroke volume with diastolic runoff widens the pulse pressure. Mitral regurgitation and mitral valve prolapse are systolic events, and aortic stenosis is a systolic ejection murmur.

questions.stem: A patient with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy is scheduled for surgery. Which change is most likely to worsen the outflow obstruction?
questions.explanation: In obstructive HCM, reduced preload, reduced afterload, tachycardia, and increased contractility all narrow the outflow tract and worsen systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflet. Management keeps the ventricle full, maintains systemic resistance with phenylephrine, and slows the heart rate, often with continued beta-blockade.

questions.stem: A patient has a new murmur and exertional dyspnea before elective surgery. Which next step is more useful than identifying whether aortic or mitral lesions are statistically more common?
options: Characterize the murmur, symptoms, and severity
Assume an aortic lesion as it is common
Assume a mitral lesion as it is common
Proceed, as prevalence does not change care
questions.explanation: A new murmur with exertional dyspnea needs characterization of the lesion, its symptoms, and its current severity, usually with echocardiography, because those findings determine perioperative significance. Knowing which lesions are statistically common does not tell you what this patient has.

questions.stem: A patient with previously severe aortic stenosis has only a 2-year-old echocardiogram and is now scheduled for elective hip replacement. Which information is most important before deciding whether to proceed?
options: Today's murmur intensity and blood pressure
Current symptoms plus an updated echo
The plan to use a spinal anesthetic
questions.explanation: Aortic stenosis progresses, so a patient with previously severe AS and a 2-year-old study needs a current symptom assessment and updated echocardiography before elective surgery, with cardiology input on valve intervention. Murmur intensity and METs alone are unreliable, and single-shot spinal is often avoided because of abrupt afterload reduction.

questions.stem: A patient with prior myocardial infarction is scheduled for suprainguinal vascular surgery and has no other classic RCRI factors. What score results?
questions.explanation: RCRI gives one point each for high-risk surgery (intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, or suprainguinal vascular), ischemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated diabetes, and creatinine above 2.0 mg/dL. Prior MI counts as ischemic heart disease and suprainguinal vascular surgery counts as high-risk surgery, so the score is 2.

questions.stem: A patient had a transient ischemic attack 6 months ago with complete recovery. Which RCRI criterion does that history satisfy?
questions.explanation: A prior stroke or transient ischemic attack satisfies the RCRI cerebrovascular disease criterion and adds 1 point even with complete recovery. It also signals systemic atherosclerosis and calls for a documented neurologic baseline.

questions.stem: Which preoperative rhythm finding is most compatible with proceeding to elective surgery when the patient is otherwise stable?
options: New atrial fibrillation with ventricular rate 140
Nonsustained ventricular tachycardia with family history of sudden death
questions.explanation: Atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular rate in an otherwise stable patient is generally compatible with elective surgery, with attention to anticoagulation and rate control. New rapid AF, SVT requiring antiarrhythmics, and nonsustained VT with a family history of sudden death all warrant evaluation first.

questions.stem: Which arrhythmia history should raise the greatest concern before elective surgery?
options: SVT on flecainide with family sudden death
questions.explanation: SVT requiring antiarrhythmic therapy, or a family history of sudden cardiac death, labels a rhythm history potentially malignant and warrants cardiology evaluation before elective surgery. Rate-controlled AF, PACs, and isolated PVCs are generally benign.

questions.stem: A patient has new palpitations and atrial fibrillation with ventricular rate 132 two days before elective knee replacement. What should happen before surgery?
options: Give one dose of metoprolol and proceed
Proceed and manage the rate intraoperatively
Start amiodarone and proceed the same day
Evaluate the new arrhythmia before proceeding
questions.explanation: New atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response before elective surgery warrants evaluation for causes such as ischemia, thyroid disease, or infection, rate control, and anticoagulation planning before proceeding. A single dose of a rate-control drug or antiarrhythmic does not address the cause or stroke risk.

questions.stem: Which four CIED details most directly determine perioperative management? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Perioperative CIED planning depends on the device type and programming, the indication, whether the patient is pacemaker-dependent with what underlying rhythm, and the date and findings of the last interrogation. Those details determine whether reprogramming, a magnet, or backup pacing is needed, while model number and generator size alone do not.

questions.stem: Monopolar cautery inhibits pacing in a pacemaker-dependent patient and the heart rate falls to 30. Which preoperative information is essential before relying on a magnet as part of the response?
options: Its battery voltage at last check
The date the leads were placed
How it behaves when one is applied
questions.explanation: Magnet behavior depends on the device and its programming; some pacemakers do not switch to asynchronous pacing with a magnet, so the team must know the magnet response and have the magnet accessible over the generator. Battery, lead dates, and sensor type do not tell you what the magnet will do.

questions.stem: Why is monopolar cautery near a pacemaker generator clinically important?
options: EMI can inhibit pacing or alter function
EMI affects ICDs but spares pacemakers
questions.explanation: Monopolar cautery near the generator creates electromagnetic interference that the device can misread as intrinsic activity, inhibiting pacing in a dependent patient or triggering inappropriate ICD therapy. EMI affects pacemakers as well as ICDs, and battery depletion and lead damage are not the main concern.

questions.stem: A pacemaker is programmed VVI. What response occurs when an intrinsic ventricular beat is sensed?
options: An atrial pacing spike is delivered
questions.explanation: In VVI mode, the device paces and senses the ventricle, and a sensed intrinsic ventricular beat inhibits the next paced output. It is a common backup mode, but it does not preserve AV synchrony.

questions.stem: A patient with AAI pacing later develops complete AV block. Why can the existing mode fail?
options: AAI paces the ventricle without sensing it
AAI relies on intact AV conduction
AAI becomes asynchronous in heart block
questions.explanation: AAI paces and senses only the atrium and relies on the patient's own AV conduction to carry each paced beat to the ventricles. With complete heart block, atrial pacing no longer produces ventricular contraction, so the patient can become severely bradycardic and needs a ventricular lead.

questions.stem: A pacemaker-dependent patient will undergo surgery with substantial monopolar cautery. Which temporary pacing strategy avoids inhibition from sensed EMI?
questions.explanation: Asynchronous modes such as VOO or DOO pace at a fixed rate without sensing, so electromagnetic interference cannot inhibit them in a pacemaker-dependent patient. The tradeoff is possible competition with intrinsic beats, which is rarely significant during surgery.

questions.stem: A dual-chamber pacemaker is intentionally placed into an asynchronous mode during a period of significant EMI risk. Which mode paces both chambers without sensing inhibition?
questions.explanation: DOO is asynchronous dual-chamber pacing. A magnet may produce asynchronous pacing in many pacemakers, but the actual response depends on the device and its programming and should not be assumed.

questions.stem: A patient with complete heart block has a device that senses atrial activity and coordinates ventricular pacing to preserve AV synchrony. Which mode best accomplishes this?
questions.explanation: DDD paces and senses both atrium and ventricle, so it tracks atrial activity and paces the ventricle after an AV delay, preserving AV synchrony in complete heart block. AAI cannot reach the ventricle through a blocked AV node, while VVI and VOO pace the ventricle without coordinating it with the atria.

questions.stem: A device is programmed VDD. Which function distinguishes this mode from DDD?
options: Senses both chambers but paces the ventricle
It paces both but senses the ventricle
It paces and senses the atrium alone
questions.explanation: VDD senses activity in both the atrium and ventricle but paces only the ventricle, tracking intrinsic atrial beats to preserve AV synchrony. Unlike DDD, it cannot pace the atrium, so it suits patients with heart block and a normal sinus node.

questions.stem: A DDDR pacemaker accelerates the paced rate when the patient becomes active despite no change in intrinsic atrial rate. Which programmed feature explains this?
questions.explanation: Rate responsiveness, the R in DDDR, uses sensors such as accelerometers or minute ventilation to raise the paced rate with activity. Minute ventilation sensors can be triggered by mechanical ventilation or monitors, causing unexpected tachycardia, so rate response is often disabled for surgery.

questions.stem: Which three therapies can an ICD deliver for tachyarrhythmias? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: ICDs treat tachyarrhythmias with antitachycardia pacing, synchronized cardioversion, and defibrillation, escalating as needed. Rate-responsive pacing treats bradycardia rather than tachycardia, ablation is a separate catheter procedure, and beta-blockade is a drug therapy.

questions.stem: Which two ICD-specific facts most directly affect the intraoperative plan? (Select 2)
options: Whether tachy therapies are active or suspended
The date of the last shock
The side of the generator pocket
questions.explanation: The intraoperative plan depends on whether the patient is pacemaker-dependent and whether tachy therapies must be suspended to avoid inappropriate shocks from electrocautery. Lead number, battery voltage, pocket side, and the last shock date matter for interrogation but do not by themselves set the intraoperative plan.

questions.stem: A patient with an ICD cannot explain why it was implanted and has no recent device records. What is the safest next step?
options: Apply a magnet and proceed without records
Assume the device is a simple pacemaker
questions.explanation: Safe planning for an ICD requires knowing why it was placed, whether the patient is pacemaker-dependent, and how the device is programmed, which device records and interrogation provide. Assuming normal function or applying a magnet without that information can leave the patient unprotected.

questions.stem: A patient with an ICD also needs bradycardia support. Which statement best reflects the device's pacing capability?
options: An ICD cannot provide bradycardia pacing
It may also provide VVI or DDD pacing
ICD pacing is limited to the atrium
questions.explanation: ICDs also function as pacemakers and are commonly programmed for bradycardia pacing in modes such as VVI or DDD. A magnet over most ICDs suspends shock therapy but does not change the pacing mode to asynchronous, so a dependent patient may need reprogramming.

questions.stem: An ICD detects ventricular tachycardia at 170 beats/min, but the patient develops sinus tachycardia to 175 during surgery. Why does that programmed threshold matter?
options: The threshold matters only after surgery
A fast normal rhythm may cause a shock
It sets the magnet response rate
It controls the backup pacing rate
questions.explanation: An ICD classifies rhythms largely by rate, so sinus tachycardia above the 170/min detection rate may be read as ventricular tachycardia and trigger an inappropriate shock. The detection rate is separate from the magnet response and the bradycardia pacing rate, and it matters during surgery.

questions.stem: An ICD was last interrogated 3 years ago and delivered two shocks last month. Which concern should take priority?
options: Device check to explain the recent therapy
The magnet response of the device
Postponing for a routine clinic visit
questions.explanation: Recent shocks may reflect new ventricular arrhythmias, ischemia, lead failure, or inappropriate therapy, and an interrogation 3 years old cannot show current function, so interrogation and evaluation of the shocks come before elective surgery. Magnet and rate-response details matter later.

questions.stem: An ICD patient will undergo monopolar cautery above the umbilicus. Which management issue is unique to the defibrillator function?
options: Whether the battery is near end of life
questions.explanation: With monopolar cautery above the umbilicus, an ICD may read interference as ventricular fibrillation and deliver a shock, so suspending tachyarrhythmia therapies, by programming or magnet, with external defibrillation ready is the issue unique to the defibrillator. Pacing settings and battery status apply to pacemakers as well.

questions.stem: A CIED patient is having a hand procedure with no electrocautery or other meaningful EMI source. Which factor becomes less central to an EMI-specific plan than it would during monopolar cautery near the generator?
questions.explanation: Distance between the surgical site and the generator matters mainly when there is an EMI source such as monopolar cautery near the device. Without a meaningful EMI source, that factor becomes less important, while pacemaker dependence, device type, and recent interrogation still matter for planning.

questions.stem: Which surgical detail most directly predicts the need for a CIED electromagnetic-interference plan?
options: Use of a peripheral nerve stimulator
questions.explanation: Monopolar electrocautery is the main intraoperative source of electromagnetic interference, especially when used near the generator, so it most directly predicts the need for a CIED plan. Bipolar cautery and ultrasonic devices produce little interference, and a nerve stimulator delivers small, brief currents.

questions.stem: A patient reports an implanted cardiac device but cannot identify whether it is a pacemaker or ICD. What should happen before a procedure in which EMI is expected?
options: Assume it is a standard pacemaker
Identify the device and its programming
Apply a magnet without identifying it
Proceed, as all devices react alike to magnets
questions.explanation: Pacemakers and ICDs respond differently to magnets and interference, so the device type, programming, and dependence must be identified from the device card, records, or interrogation before a procedure with expected EMI. Assuming the most common device type can leave the patient unprotected.

questions.stem: Spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 0.55 in a patient with COPD. Which anesthetic implication follows most directly?
options: Normal airflow with reduced lung volumes
Obstruction with limited reserve and reactivity
Fully reversible obstruction without added risk
questions.explanation: An FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.55 indicates obstructive physiology, which in COPD means limited ventilatory reserve, air trapping, and reactive airways prone to bronchospasm during instrumentation. Restrictive disease shows a normal or high ratio with reduced volumes.

questions.stem: A COPD patient's baseline ABG is pH 7.37, PaCO2 52, PaO2 62, HCO3 30. Which interpretation best fits the compensated pattern?
options: Normal gas exchange for the patient's age
questions.explanation: A near-normal pH with PaCO2 52 and bicarbonate 30 indicates chronic respiratory acidosis with renal compensation, and PaO2 62 shows baseline hypoxemia. Knowing this baseline guides ventilation targets, since normalizing PaCO2 can cause alkalosis, and helps set extubation expectations.

questions.stem: A COPD patient has hyperinflated lungs and large bullae on chest imaging. Which anesthetic concern follows most directly?
options: The findings exclude concern for air trapping
Barotrauma risk; nitrous oxide may expand them
The findings indicate cardiogenic pulmonary edema
High tidal volumes are needed to reopen alveoli
questions.explanation: Large bullae can rupture with positive-pressure ventilation, causing pneumothorax, and nitrous oxide diffuses into closed gas spaces and enlarges them. Ventilation uses modest tidal volumes and pressures with a long expiratory time to limit air trapping and barotrauma.

questions.stem: A COPD patient is actively wheezing in preop and has not used a bronchodilator since yesterday. What should occur before induction?
options: Treat bronchospasm with inhaled bronchodilator therapy
Proceed and treat only after intubation
Delay all surgery for six weeks
Rely on volatile anesthetic after induction as the first treatment
questions.explanation: Active wheezing before induction should be treated with an inhaled beta-2 agonist so airway reactivity is reduced before instrumentation, which is a strong bronchospasm trigger. Waiting until after intubation risks severe bronchospasm, and volatile agents are an adjunct rather than the first treatment.

questions.stem: Which three inhaler details are most useful for judging pulmonary control before surgery? (Select 3)
options: When the last dose was taken
questions.explanation: Which inhalers are prescribed, how often they are used, and when the last dose was taken show disease severity and current control, since increasing rescue use signals poor control. Technique matters for effectiveness, and spacer brand and refills do not describe current control.

questions.stem: A patient has episodic wheezing that returns to baseline after bronchodilator therapy and is triggered by allergens and exercise. Which physiology best fits the history?
questions.explanation: Episodic wheezing triggered by allergens or exercise that returns to baseline after bronchodilator therapy reflects reversible airflow obstruction, the hallmark of asthma. COPD shows largely fixed obstruction, and restrictive disease reduces lung volumes rather than airflow.

questions.stem: Which four factors are recognized asthma triggers and therefore relevant to preoperative control? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Exercise, respiratory infections, emotional stress, and allergens are common asthma triggers, so asking about them helps judge control and plan around avoidable triggers. Cold, dry air rather than warm humidified air provokes bronchospasm, and adequate hydration is not a trigger.

questions.stem: A patient with asthma uses inhaled fluticasone and albuterol. What is the best morning-of-surgery medication plan?
options: Replace inhalers with oral steroids on the day of surgery
questions.explanation: Inhaled steroids and bronchodilators are continued on the morning of surgery to keep airway reactivity controlled. Stopping them can increase the risk of bronchospasm during airway instrumentation. Replacing them with oral steroids that morning does not provide the same immediate airway effect.

questions.stem: A patient completed a prednisone taper last month. Which perioperative issue should be considered if exposure was sufficient to suppress the HPA axis?
questions.explanation: Recent systemic steroid courses can suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis for months, risking adrenal insufficiency and refractory hypotension under surgical stress. Patients with likely suppression may receive stress-dose hydrocortisone, scaled to the size of the procedure.

questions.stem: A patient's asthma is strongly stress-triggered and she is very anxious before surgery. Why may anxiolysis help reduce respiratory risk?
questions.explanation: Emotional stress is a recognized asthma trigger, so treating marked anxiety can lower the chance of bronchospasm at induction. Anxiolytics do not bronchodilate, replace controller inhalers, or dry secretions.

questions.stem: An adult recently recovered from a URI but still has cough and airway irritability before an elective case requiring airway instrumentation. What is the key planning issue?
options: Reactivity ends once the fever resolves
Every adult URI needs a fixed 6-week delay
A normal SpO2 removes the added airway risk
questions.explanation: Airway hyperreactivity after a viral URI can persist for up to about 6 weeks, increasing the risk of bronchospasm and laryngospasm with instrumentation. Timing is individualized to residual symptoms, the airway plan, urgency, and patient factors rather than a rigid rule.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old has mild clear rhinorrhea, no fever, and normal activity before ear tubes. Which distinction makes proceeding more reasonable than in an adult with an active URI?
options: A chest radiograph excludes anesthetic risk
Children do not develop airway hyperreactivity
Pediatric URIs carry less risk than adult URIs
Mild afebrile URI may be judged case by case
questions.explanation: Children have frequent URIs, so a mild, afebrile illness with clear secretions and normal activity is often managed case by case, especially for short procedures like ear tubes. Fever, purulent secretions, lower respiratory signs, or lethargy favor postponement, since children do develop airway hyperreactivity.

questions.stem: A child with a current URI is having surgery. Which factor most increases the risk of perioperative respiratory adverse events?
questions.explanation: In children with a URI, endotracheal intubation raises the risk of laryngospasm, bronchospasm, and desaturation more than a face mask or supraglottic airway. Other risk factors include age under about 2 years, airway surgery, copious secretions, prematurity, reactive airway disease, and parental smoking.

questions.stem: Which three assessments belong in routine pulmonary screening for an obese patient who snores? (Select 3)
options: History of diagnosed OSA and CPAP use
questions.explanation: For an obese patient who snores, pulmonary screening includes STOP-BANG, any diagnosed OSA with CPAP use and settings, and auscultation of the heart and lungs. Peak flow, chest CT, and blood gases are ordered for specific indications such as asthma, lung masses, or suspected hypercapnia.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man snores, is tired, has hypertension, BMI 33, neck circumference 42 cm, and is male. No apnea has been observed. Using the traditional STOP-BANG scoring thresholds, what is the score?
questions.explanation: Using the traditional STOP-BANG thresholds: snoring, tiredness, hypertension, age over 50, neck circumference over 40 cm, and male sex each score 1, for a total of 6. BMI 33 does not meet the traditional >35 threshold and no witnessed apnea is reported.

questions.stem: Using the traditional STOP-BANG scoring thresholds, a 48-year-old woman has BMI 37, neck circumference 38 cm, and hypertension. Which criteria are positive?
questions.explanation: Using the traditional STOP-BANG thresholds, BMI over 35 and hypertension are positive. Age 48 does not meet the over-50 criterion, and a 38-cm neck does not meet the traditional over-40-cm criterion.

questions.stem: A patient with moderate OSA uses CPAP nightly and is scheduled for outpatient knee arthroscopy. Which preoperative instruction is most appropriate?
options: Stop CPAP the night before surgery
Leave CPAP at home, as PACU has oxygen
Bring the CPAP device for use after surgery
Resume CPAP only after the first week
questions.explanation: Patients with OSA should bring their own CPAP and use it postoperatively, especially when sleeping or receiving opioids, because anesthetics and opioids worsen airway collapse. Supplemental oxygen alone can mask hypoventilation without treating obstruction, and adherent patients with controlled comorbidities can often have outpatient surgery.

questions.stem: A patient has a STOP-BANG score of 4. What is the most useful perioperative implication?
options: No precautions until a sleep study confirms OSA
The score diagnoses OSA and requires cancellation
The score excludes severe obstructive sleep apnea
Meaningful risk that should shape the plan
questions.explanation: A STOP-BANG score of 3 to 4 indicates intermediate risk of OSA, which should prompt opioid-sparing analgesia, cautious sedation, airway preparation, and closer postoperative monitoring. The score screens rather than diagnoses, and elective surgery does not have to wait for a sleep study in most patients.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman snores, is tired, has witnessed apnea, hypertension, and BMI 37. What STOP-BANG risk category does this produce?
options: High risk with a score of 6
Intermediate risk with a score of 4
Low risk with a score of 2
Intermediate risk with a score of 5
questions.explanation: Snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, hypertension, BMI over 35, and age over 50 each score 1 point, for a total of 6, and a score of 5 to 8 is high risk. Neck circumference and male sex do not apply here, so scores of 4 or 5 undercount the positive items.

questions.stem: A young patient has only one positive STOP-BANG item. What can be concluded from the screening tool?
options: Low score; clinical judgment still applies
The score replaces the airway assessment
questions.explanation: A low STOP-BANG score lowers the probability of OSA but does not rule it out, so clinical findings such as witnessed apneas or a difficult airway still matter. The score does not replace airway assessment or decisions about postoperative monitoring.

questions.stem: Which three STOP-BANG components are based on patient characteristics or measurements rather than symptoms? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: BMI, neck circumference, and age are measured or demographic items in STOP-BANG, along with male gender. Snoring, tiredness, and observed apnea are reported symptoms, and pressure refers to a hypertension diagnosis.

questions.stem: A patient who smokes a pack a day is scheduled for elective lung resection in 10 weeks. What is the best advice about smoking cessation?
options: Quit only during the final 24 hours
Keep smoking to avoid increased secretions
Quit now; benefits grow with longer abstinence
Cut down by half without fully quitting
questions.explanation: Quitting several weeks or more before surgery reduces pulmonary and wound complications, with greater benefit at about 4 to 8 weeks or longer, and even 12 to 24 hours of abstinence lowers carboxyhemoglobin. Concern that short-term quitting increases complications has not been supported, so cessation is encouraged at any time.

questions.stem: A patient denies smoking cigarettes but reports daily vaping. What is the best preoperative history approach?
options: Treat vaping as identical to cigarette exposure in every respect
Ignore vaping because it carries no airway relevance
Assume vaping is declining and less important than cigarettes
Ask directly about vaping because it may otherwise be missed
questions.explanation: Patients who do not consider themselves smokers may not mention e-cigarettes, so vaping should be asked about directly, since it is increasingly common. Vaping can cause airway irritation and, rarely, acute lung injury, but its risks are not identical to cigarettes, so the history guides rather than replaces assessment.

questions.stem: A patient with asthma has needed the rescue inhaler repeatedly this week. Which conclusion should drive elective-surgery planning?
options: Control is poor and should be optimized before surgery
Frequent rescue use indicates adequate control
The disease is mild and requires no plan change
A fixed six-week postponement is mandatory
questions.explanation: Repeated rescue inhaler use within a week means asthma is poorly controlled, which raises the risk of bronchospasm during airway instrumentation. Elective surgery is better deferred while maintenance therapy is adjusted, sometimes with a short steroid course, rather than following a fixed postponement interval.

questions.stem: An adult with a mild URI must proceed with surgery today. Which airway choice best reduces the risk of perioperative bronchospasm, if the procedure allows it?
options: A supraglottic airway instead of intubation
questions.explanation: When surgery cannot be delayed in a patient with a recent URI, avoiding the trachea with a supraglottic airway or face mask lowers the risk of bronchospasm and laryngospasm compared with an endotracheal tube. If intubation is needed, adequate depth and a bronchodilator beforehand help, while instrumentation under light anesthesia is a strong trigger.

questions.stem: A COPD patient on tiotropium, a long-acting inhaled anticholinergic, asks about inhalers on the morning of surgery. What is the best advice?
options: Use all usual inhalers, including tiotropium
Hold all inhalers once NPO begins
Use the rescue inhaler alone that morning
questions.explanation: Maintenance inhalers, including long-acting anticholinergics, long-acting beta agonists, and inhaled steroids, should be taken on the morning of surgery and brought to the hospital. Stopping them increases the risk of bronchospasm and worsening obstruction, and inhaled doses are compatible with fasting rules.

questions.stem: During colectomy, a diabetic patient's glucose rises from 168 to 214 mg/dL. Which response best balances treatment of stress hyperglycemia against unnecessary delay?
options: Postpone the operation since it exceeds 200 mg/dL
Treat, since it exceeds the 180 mg/dL threshold
Wait to treat until glucose exceeds 250 mg/dL
Treat only once urine ketones become positive
questions.explanation: Perioperative glucose above about 180 mg/dL is generally treated with insulin because sustained hyperglycemia increases infection and impaired healing. Mild intraoperative hyperglycemia from surgical stress does not justify stopping an operation, and waiting for ketones delays treatment.

questions.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes has a morning glucose of 325 mg/dL before elective hernia repair. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Consider postponement for better glucose control
Proceed routinely with an insulin infusion
Give one insulin dose and proceed once below 300 mg/dL
Cancel permanently and refer for long-term management
questions.explanation: A morning glucose above about 300 mg/dL before elective surgery may warrant postponement, especially with ketones, dehydration, or a high HbA1c, because severe hyperglycemia increases infection, fluid shifts, and metabolic complications. Rapidly lowering the value with one insulin dose does not correct the underlying poor control.

questions.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes takes glipizide and NPH insulin. Which morning-of-surgery plan best limits both fasting hypoglycemia and excessive hyperglycemia?
options: Take both at their usual full doses
Give full NPH; hold the glipizide
Hold glipizide; give half the NPH dose
Hold both until glucose is checked
questions.explanation: Sulfonylureas such as glipizide stimulate insulin release and can cause hypoglycemia while fasting, so they are held the morning of surgery. About half the usual NPH dose provides basal insulin and limits hyperglycemia, while a full dose risks hypoglycemia and holding all insulin invites hyperglycemia and ketosis.

questions.stem: Which three laboratory values most directly help assess chronic diabetic control, current glucose status, and a common end-organ complication before surgery? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: HbA1c reflects glucose control over about 3 months, the morning glucose shows the current state, and renal function screens for diabetic nephropathy, which affects drug dosing and fluid plans. TSH, lipase, and cortisol are ordered only for specific indications.

questions.stem: A diabetic patient's glucose rises from 140 to 238 mg/dL after dexamethasone 8 mg for PONV prophylaxis. Which explanation is most likely?
options: The steroid raises it for about a day
questions.explanation: Dexamethasone raises blood glucose for up to about 24 hours by increasing gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance, with a larger effect in diabetic patients. Glucose should be rechecked after it is given, while fasting tends to lower glucose and ondansetron does not affect it.

questions.stem: Which four comorbid conditions should be actively sought in a patient with long-standing diabetes because they may alter anesthetic management? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Long-standing diabetes is associated with hypertension, coronary artery disease that may be silent, peripheral vascular disease, nephropathy, and autonomic neuropathy with delayed gastric emptying that increases aspiration risk. Hyperthyroidism and asthma are not characteristic complications.

questions.stem: A patient with an insulin pump is scheduled for a 4-hour prone spine case using fluoroscopy and electrocautery. Which three considerations most directly determine whether the pump can remain in use? (Select 3)
options: Radiation, magnetic fields, and electrocautery exposure
Time since the last site change
questions.explanation: Whether an insulin pump can stay on depends on procedure length, positioning and access to the site, and exposure to radiation, magnetic fields, or electrocautery. Long prone cases with fluoroscopy often favor switching to an insulin infusion, while insulin concentration, alarm volume, and site age do not drive that decision.

questions.stem: A patient with a CGM and insulin pump is scheduled for MRI-guided surgery. Which device concern should be anticipated?
options: The CGM and pump may need removal for MRI
The pump removes the need for glucose checks
The pump basal rate should be raised
Both devices can stay in place during MRI
questions.explanation: Insulin pumps and continuous glucose monitors are generally not MRI safe, so they are removed before MRI exposure and glucose is managed with point-of-care checks and IV insulin as needed. The basal rate is not routinely increased, and a pump does not replace glucose monitoring.

questions.stem: A nondiabetic patient develops glucose 168 mg/dL during major surgery despite fasting and no dextrose infusion. Which mechanism best explains this?
options: Stress hormones raise glucose and resistance
The value is most likely a laboratory error
questions.explanation: Surgical stress releases catecholamines, cortisol, and glucagon, which increase hepatic glucose output and insulin resistance, so glucose rises even in fasting nondiabetic patients. Fasting tends to lower glucose, and anesthetics do not stop insulin secretion entirely.

questions.stem: A patient with well-controlled hypothyroidism takes levothyroxine and is NPO for elective surgery. Which medication plan is most appropriate?
options: Hold levothyroxine because all oral medications are prohibited while NPO
Stop levothyroxine for one week to avoid intraoperative tachycardia
questions.explanation: Levothyroxine should be continued on the morning of surgery with a sip of water, since oral medications are allowed under fasting rules. Its long half-life of about 7 days means a missed dose has little immediate effect, but stopping it serves no purpose.

questions.stem: A patient with hyperthyroidism takes propylthiouracil and propranolol. Which morning-of-surgery plan best reduces risk of thyroid-related hemodynamic instability?
questions.explanation: Antithyroid drugs such as propylthiouracil and beta-blockers such as propranolol are continued on the morning of surgery to maintain control and prevent tachycardia or thyroid storm. Holding either one removes protection during the stress of surgery.

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for elective hernia repair has HR 128, tremor, weight loss, and undetectable TSH. Which issue should drive the decision to postpone?
options: Minor surgery does not require euthyroid status
A beta-blocker bolus makes immediate surgery equivalent to optimization
Regional anesthesia eliminates the thyroid-related risk
Poorly controlled hyperthyroidism increases perioperative instability risk
questions.explanation: Tachycardia, tremor, weight loss, and a suppressed TSH indicate uncontrolled hyperthyroidism, which risks thyroid storm and arrhythmias with surgical stress, so elective surgery is postponed until the patient is euthyroid. Beta-blockade alone and regional anesthesia do not remove this risk.

questions.stem: Which hemodynamic and pharmacologic pattern is most consistent with significant hypothyroidism during anesthesia?
questions.explanation: Significant hypothyroidism reduces cardiac output and blunts baroreflexes, so patients are prone to hypotension, and slowed hepatic metabolism prolongs drug effects. Hypothermia and delayed emergence are common, while tachycardia, hyperthermia, and hypertension point to hyperthyroidism.

questions.stem: A patient with known hypothyroidism is taking levothyroxine. Which test best confirms whether replacement therapy is adequately controlling the disorder before elective surgery?
questions.explanation: In primary hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine, TSH is the best test of adequate replacement, since a normal value indicates euthyroid status. Free T3 alone is less reliable, cortisol assesses adrenal function, and ultrasound shows structure rather than function.

questions.stem: Which glucocorticoid history most strongly raises concern for clinically meaningful HPA-axis suppression before surgery?
options: Prednisone 5 mg for one day six months ago
A single dexamethasone dose for postoperative nausea prophylaxis
Prednisone 20 mg daily for several weeks with recent use
Low-potency topical hydrocortisone used briefly on a small area
questions.explanation: Risk of HPA-axis suppression depends on glucocorticoid dose, duration, route, timing, and patient factors. Sustained systemic prednisone at moderate-to-high doses is substantially more concerning than a single dose or brief low-dose exposure.

questions.stem: A chronic steroid user develops profound hypotension after induction. Fluids and escalating vasopressors produce little response, and there is no rash, wheeze, or major blood loss. Which diagnosis should now move highest on the differential?
questions.explanation: Chronic glucocorticoid exposure can suppress the HPA axis and prevent an adequate cortisol response to surgical stress. Hypotension that stays refractory to fluids and vasopressors without signs of anaphylaxis or bleeding should prompt consideration of adrenal insufficiency and treatment with hydrocortisone.

questions.stem: A patient with Addison disease presents with hypotension, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. Which treatment addresses the underlying endocrine problem rather than only supporting blood pressure?
questions.explanation: Addison disease causes cortisol and aldosterone deficiency, producing hypotension, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia, so treatment is hydrocortisone replacement with correction of fluids and electrolytes. Fluids and vasopressors only support pressure, and potassium supplements would worsen hyperkalemia.

questions.stem: Which two findings are most consistent with cortisol excess in Cushing syndrome? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Cortisol excess in Cushing syndrome causes sodium and fluid retention with hypervolemia and hypertension, and its mineralocorticoid effect produces hypokalemia. Hyperkalemia, hypotension, and hypoglycemia are features of adrenal insufficiency, the opposite condition.

questions.stem: A patient with pheochromocytoma is scheduled for adrenalectomy. Which preoperative preparation is most important?
options: ACE inhibitor as the first agent
questions.explanation: Pheochromocytoma preparation begins with alpha-blockade, such as phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin, for about 1 to 2 weeks with liberal fluid and salt, and beta-blockade is added only afterward. Beta-blockade first leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, fluid restriction worsens volume contraction, and ACE inhibitors do not control catecholamine surges.

questions.stem: A patient with primary hyperaldosteronism reaches adrenalectomy with persistent hypertension and potassium 2.8 mEq/L. Which abnormality most directly increases immediate anesthetic risk?
options: Cortisol deficiency causing refractory vasodilatory shock before gland removal
Catecholamine release causing classic tumor-manipulation hypertensive crises
Hypokalemia predisposing to dysrhythmias and altered neuromuscular-blocker response
questions.explanation: Primary hyperaldosteronism commonly produces hypertension and hypokalemia. Significant hypokalemia increases dysrhythmia risk and can alter neuromuscular-blocker effects. Tumor-manipulation catecholamine surges are characteristic of pheochromocytoma, not Conn syndrome.

questions.stem: A patient takes prednisone 10 mg daily chronically and is having a superficial skin procedure under local anesthesia. Which steroid plan is most appropriate?
options: Withhold the dose on surgery day
questions.explanation: For superficial procedures under local anesthesia, the usual daily glucocorticoid dose is enough and no supplement is needed. Supplemental hydrocortisone is scaled to the stress of larger operations, and withholding the usual dose risks adrenal insufficiency.

questions.stem: A patient taking chronic glucocorticoids is having inguinal hernia repair. Which principle best guides perioperative steroid management?
options: Continue the usual dose; tailor supplements
Give 50 mg hydrocortisone to every steroid user
Stop the usual steroid on the day of surgery
Give 100 mg plus 200 mg/day for minor surgery
questions.explanation: Current practice avoids a single large stress-dose regimen for every chronic steroid user. The usual glucocorticoid is generally continued, while supplemental parenteral hydrocortisone is tailored to the likelihood of HPA-axis suppression, oral intake, and surgical stress.

questions.stem: A patient takes prednisone 5 mg daily. What is the approximate equivalent dose of hydrocortisone?
questions.explanation: Prednisone is about 4 times as potent as hydrocortisone as a glucocorticoid, so 5 mg of prednisone is roughly equal to 20 mg of hydrocortisone, near normal daily cortisol production. Dexamethasone is about 25 times as potent as hydrocortisone, with little mineralocorticoid effect.

questions.stem: A chronic glucocorticoid user with probable HPA-axis suppression is scheduled for major surgery and cannot take the usual oral dose perioperatively. Which principle is most appropriate?
options: Use the small dose used for superficial cases
Give parenteral coverage scaled to major stress
Permanently stop the steroid after surgery
questions.explanation: Patients with probable HPA-axis suppression who cannot take their usual glucocorticoid need parenteral coverage scaled to surgical stress, then a return toward their baseline regimen as they recover. Withholding steroids until hypotension develops risks adrenal crisis.

questions.stem: After perioperative supplemental glucocorticoids are no longer required, what is the appropriate goal for a patient who remains on chronic steroid therapy?
options: Taper the patient's chronic maintenance steroid to zero solely because surgery is complete
Continue high-dose hydrocortisone for two weeks regardless of recovery
Return to the patient's baseline chronic regimen as oral intake and clinical status permit
questions.explanation: Supplemental perioperative glucocorticoids are reduced as surgical stress resolves, while patients who require chronic therapy return to their baseline regimen. The exact transition is individualized rather than governed by a universal 50%-per-day rule.

questions.stem: A patient has chronic fatigue, weight loss, hyperpigmentation, hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and low cortisol. Which diagnosis best unifies these findings?
questions.explanation: Low cortisol with hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hyperpigmentation points to primary adrenal insufficiency, Addison disease, in which loss of feedback raises ACTH and causes the pigmentation. Cushing and Conn syndromes cause hypertension and hypokalemia, and pheochromocytoma causes catecholamine excess.

questions.stem: A patient takes oral prednisone for an inflammatory condition before surgery. Which three history details most directly determine the risk of HPA-axis suppression? (Select 3)
options: How recently the last dose was taken
The disease the steroid is treating
Whether a stress dose was given at a prior surgery
questions.explanation: HPA suppression depends on glucocorticoid exposure: dose, duration, and how recently it was taken, so prednisone of 20 mg or more daily for over 3 weeks within the past year raises concern. The underlying disease, glucose level, and prior stress dosing are relevant history but do not by themselves determine whether the axis is suppressed now.

questions.stem: A diabetic patient becomes symptomatic when glucose reaches about 60 mg/dL. Why is that personal threshold worth documenting before anesthesia?
options: It flags hypoglycemia masked by anesthesia
It sets the intraoperative insulin infusion rate
It defines the patient's target glucose range
It predicts the risk of postoperative delirium
questions.explanation: Knowing the glucose level at which a patient feels symptoms, and how low values have gone, helps the team anticipate hypoglycemia, because sedation and anesthesia hide its warning signs. It does not set the insulin rate or target range, and it does not predict delirium.

questions.stem: One diabetic patient has glucose 58 mg/dL and another has glucose 310 mg/dL in preop. Which paired treatment best addresses the immediate metabolic problems?
questions.explanation: Glucose of 58 mg/dL is hypoglycemia and is treated with IV dextrose, while 310 mg/dL is marked hyperglycemia treated with insulin and evaluation for ketosis, possibly postponing elective surgery. Leaving 310 untreated for hours or giving the same drug to both patients is wrong.

questions.stem: A diabetic patient's glucose remains above 250 mg/dL throughout a long case. Which postoperative consequence becomes more likely?
questions.explanation: Sustained perioperative hyperglycemia impairs neutrophil function and collagen synthesis, raising the risk of surgical site infection and poor wound healing. It does not cause delayed emergence or prolonged blockade, and hypoglycemia is the opposite problem.

questions.stem: A patient drank plain black coffee at 0700 for a 0930 case. Under ASA fasting guidelines, how should this be interpreted?
questions.explanation: Black coffee without milk or creamer is a clear liquid with a 2-hour fasting requirement, so 2.5 hours from 0700 to 0930 is adequate. Adding milk changes it to a non-human milk requiring 6 hours.

questions.stem: An infant received formula at 0400 and breast milk at 0500 for a 0930 case. Which intake determines whether fasting is adequate?
options: The breast milk, since 4 hours have passed
The breast milk, which needs 6 hours
questions.explanation: Breast milk requires 4 hours and infant formula requires 6 hours of fasting. The formula at 0400 is the limiting intake, and 0400 to 0930 is only 5.5 hours, so fasting is not yet adequate.

questions.stem: Which drink, taken 2 hours before an elective anesthetic, meets the clear-liquid fasting guideline?
questions.explanation: Clear liquids, which require 2 hours, include water, pulp-free juice, carbonated drinks, clear tea, black coffee, and sports drinks. Juice with pulp, milk added to coffee, and anything containing solids are not clear liquids and follow longer fasting times.

questions.stem: A patient ate plain toast at 0500 for an 1100 case. Which fasting interpretation is correct?
options: A light meal requires only 4 hours
Six hours is adequate for a light meal
questions.explanation: A light meal such as toast and clear liquid requires 6 hours of fasting, so 0500 to 1100 is adequate. Fried or fatty foods and meat require 8 hours or more because they empty from the stomach more slowly.

questions.stem: A patient ate bacon and eggs at 0600 for a 1200 case. Why is six hours insufficient?
options: Fatty meals need 8 hours to empty
Six hours is adequate for any meal
Any meal with protein requires 24 hours
questions.explanation: Heavy meals with fried or fatty foods or meat slow gastric emptying and require 8 hours or more of fasting, so 6 hours is not enough. Light meals such as toast need 6 hours, and no meal requires 24 hours under the guidelines.

questions.stem: A properly fasted patient is found chewing gum shortly before elective induction. Which physiologic effect explains why gum use still matters during the aspiration-risk assessment?
options: Chewing converts gastric contents into particulate material
Chewing reliably accelerates gastric emptying enough to negate fasting
questions.explanation: Chewing gum stimulates saliva and gastric acid secretion, but studies show little change in aspiration risk, so many facilities ask the patient to remove it rather than cancel the case. The gum itself must be removed to avoid aspirating it.

questions.stem: A patient sucked on hard candy one hour before induction. Why is this not treated like a clear liquid?
options: Candy is a clear liquid once dissolved
Dissolved candy counts as a solid
questions.explanation: Hard candy dissolves into a sugar-containing material that is treated as solid or particulate rather than a clear liquid, so it does not fit the 2-hour clear-liquid rule. It does not raise gastric pH or speed emptying, and many institutions apply the solid-food interval.

questions.stem: Which three medications most directly reduce aspiration injury risk by decreasing gastric volume, increasing emptying, or reducing acidity? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide speeds gastric emptying and raises lower esophageal sphincter tone, famotidine reduces acid secretion, and nonparticulate sodium citrate neutralizes existing acid. Magnesium sulfate, promethazine, and scopolamine do not reduce gastric volume or acidity.

questions.stem: Why is sodium citrate preferred over a particulate magnesium-aluminum antacid for aspiration prophylaxis before cesarean delivery?
options: It coats the stomach as a particulate barrier
questions.explanation: Sodium citrate is a nonparticulate antacid, so if aspirated it causes much less lung injury than particulate magnesium-aluminum antacids, which can cause severe pneumonitis. It raises gastric pH quickly but does not reduce volume or speed emptying.

questions.stem: Which THREE conditions keep aspiration risk elevated even when standard fasting times are met? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Gastroparesis and obstruction leave gastric contents in place despite fasting, and pregnancy lowers lower esophageal sphincter tone and slows emptying. A clear carbohydrate drink and black coffee are clear liquids that empty normally after 2 hours, and chewing gum is not a reason to delay an elective case under current guidance.

questions.stem: A patient taking weekly semaglutide has satisfied standard fasting intervals but reports early satiety and intermittent nausea. Which assumption is least safe?
options: Standard NPO time alone proves the stomach is empty
The medication may delay gastric emptying
Symptoms may increase concern for retained gastric contents
Aspiration risk assessment should extend beyond elapsed fasting time
questions.explanation: GLP-1 receptor agonists can delay gastric emptying, and gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, bloating, or early satiety increase concern for retained gastric contents. Meeting a clock-based fasting interval therefore does not by itself establish an empty stomach or low aspiration risk.

questions.stem: A semaglutide user remains nauseated and bloated after 10 hours of fasting. Which bedside test can directly help assess residual gastric contents?
questions.explanation: Gastric point-of-care ultrasound of the antrum can show whether the stomach is empty or contains fluid or solids, which guides decisions such as delaying or using rapid sequence induction. Radiographs, CT, and contrast studies are impractical and expose the patient to radiation without better bedside answers.

questions.stem: Which two complications can result from unnecessarily prolonged preoperative fasting? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Unnecessarily long fasting causes dehydration with hypotension at induction and hypoglycemia, especially in children and diabetic patients. It does not lower aspiration risk, and its links to pain, prolonged blockade, or urinary retention are not established, so patients are encouraged to drink clear liquids until 2 hours before surgery.

questions.stem: A patient with small-bowel obstruction has been NPO for 10 hours and needs urgent surgery. Which principle should guide airway planning?
options: Ten hours of fasting makes risk low
questions.explanation: Mechanical bowel obstruction retains large volumes of fluid and particulate material proximal to the blockage despite many hours without oral intake. The patient is treated as having high aspiration risk, typically with gastric decompression and rapid sequence induction.

questions.stem: Two patients have both fasted for 10 hours. One is healthy; the other has symptomatic gastroparesis. Why should their aspiration plans differ?
options: Once fasting exceeds 8 hours, gastric contents are predictably absent
Elapsed fasting time determines aspiration risk independent of comorbidity
Gastroparesis matters only when fasting is shorter than 8 hours
Disease can cause retained gastric contents despite identical fasting duration
questions.explanation: Fasting recommendations assume reasonably normal gastric emptying. Gastroparesis violates that assumption, so clinically important residual gastric contents may remain after the same fasting interval that is adequate for a healthy patient; aspiration planning must account for the underlying disorder.

questions.stem: Why is pregnancy treated as an aspiration-risk condition in preoperative planning?
options: It raises risk despite proper fasting
It raises lower esophageal sphincter tone
Proper fasting fully removes the risk
Risk applies only during active labor
questions.explanation: Progesterone relaxes the lower esophageal sphincter, and the gravid uterus raises intragastric pressure and displaces the stomach, so aspiration risk stays elevated despite fasting, typically from mid-pregnancy. Sphincter tone falls rather than rises, and the risk is not limited to labor.

questions.stem: A healthy elective patient asks why fasting is required when modern airway devices are available. Which complication are the fasting intervals primarily designed to reduce?
questions.explanation: Fasting guidelines aim to reduce the volume and acidity of gastric contents and so lower the risk of pulmonary aspiration, which airway devices do not reliably prevent. Fasting does not prevent PONV or ileus, and prolonged fasting can actually cause hypoglycemia.

questions.stem: A patient drank pulp-free apple juice 2.5 hours before surgery. Which fasting interpretation is correct?
options: Acceptable; pulp-free juice is a clear liquid
Acceptable only if under 100 mL was taken
questions.explanation: Pulp-free juice is a clear liquid with a 2-hour fasting requirement, so 2.5 hours is adequate. Juice with pulp is not clear and is treated like a light meal at 6 hours, which is the tempting confusion. ASA guidance does not set a volume cutoff for clear liquids taken more than 2 hours before.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetic gastroparesis ate a light meal 6 hours ago. Why should this not be treated as a routine 6-hour fast?
options: All diabetic patients need a 24-hour fast
Contents may remain; consider ultrasound or delay
Six hours guarantees an empty stomach
Clear liquids now will lower aspiration risk
questions.explanation: Standard fasting intervals assume normal gastric emptying, which diabetic gastroparesis violates, so clinically important contents may remain after a nominal 6-hour fast. Symptoms, gastric ultrasound, delay, or rapid sequence induction may change the plan.

questions.stem: Why can current fasting instructions allow clear liquids until 2 hours before anesthesia instead of requiring 'nothing after midnight' for everyone?
options: Modern guidelines permit a shorter clear-liquid interval
Clear liquids carry zero aspiration risk
The shorter interval applies only to healthy adults
questions.explanation: Evidence showed that clear liquids empty from the stomach within about 2 hours and that drinking them until then does not increase gastric volume or aspiration risk, so guidelines replaced blanket nothing-after-midnight rules. Shorter fasting also reduces thirst, dehydration, and hypoglycemia, though no interval makes the risk zero.

questions.stem: A trauma patient in severe pain has been NPO for 10 hours. Why can aspiration risk remain elevated?
options: Ten hours of fasting eliminates retained gastric contents
Pain lowers gastric acidity enough to prevent injury
questions.explanation: Severe pain, trauma, stress, and opioids slow gastric emptying, so a trauma patient can retain gastric contents despite many hours without intake. Such patients are treated as having a full stomach, usually with rapid sequence induction.

questions.stem: A patient with BMI 44 and active GERD needs urgent laparoscopy. Which prophylactic approach best reduces the severity of potential aspiration?
options: A PPI given at induction of anesthesia
An H2 blocker plus a nonparticulate antacid
questions.explanation: Obesity and active GERD raise aspiration risk, so an H2 blocker such as famotidine reduces acid production and a nonparticulate antacid such as sodium citrate raises gastric pH at induction, along with RSI. A particulate antacid injures the lungs if aspirated, a PPI at induction is too slow, and ondansetron does not reduce acidity.

questions.stem: A patient ate a cheeseburger and fries 7 hours before elective anesthesia. Which decision best applies the fasting guideline?
options: Delay until 12 hours because any fried food requires that interval
Proceed because all solid food requires only 6 hours
Proceed because meat is treated as a light meal
Delay because a fatty meal requires at least 8 hours
questions.explanation: A cheeseburger and fries is a fatty meal with meat, which requires at least 8 hours of fasting, so 7 hours is not enough for elective anesthesia. The 6-hour interval applies to light meals, and no standard guideline requires 12 hours for fried food.

questions.stem: Which metabolic condition can prolong gastric emptying and therefore increase aspiration risk despite standard fasting?
questions.explanation: Hypothyroidism slows gastrointestinal motility and gastric emptying, making it a metabolic cause of retained contents despite standard fasting. Pregnancy, GI obstruction, and GERD also raise aspiration risk, but through hormonal, mechanical, or sphincter mechanisms rather than metabolic slowing.

questions.stem: A cirrhotic patient with tense ascites and encephalopathy requires urgent surgery. Which airway strategy best addresses the aspiration risk?
questions.explanation: Tense ascites raises intra-abdominal pressure and encephalopathy impairs protective reflexes, so this patient has high aspiration risk and rapid sequence induction with a cuffed endotracheal tube is appropriate. Mask induction and supraglottic airways do not protect the airway from regurgitated contents.

questions.stem: Which four variables are components of the Child-Pugh score? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: The Child-Pugh score uses bilirubin, albumin, INR or prothrombin time, ascites, and encephalopathy, each graded 1 to 3 points. Sodium appears in MELD-Na, and platelet count is not part of either score.

questions.stem: A cirrhotic patient has bilirubin 3.1, INR 1.9, creatinine 1.6, sodium 128, albumin 2.6, and ascites. Which values are used in the MELD calculation?
questions.explanation: MELD-Na is calculated from bilirubin, INR, creatinine, and sodium, all objective laboratory values. Albumin, ascites, and encephalopathy are part of Child-Pugh, which includes subjective clinical grading.

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis has a MELD score of 17 and is being evaluated for elective nonhepatic surgery. Which additional step is generally recommended?
options: Correct the INR and then proceed
Proceed, since referral starts at MELD 25
Use Child-Pugh alone for nonhepatic cases
questions.explanation: A MELD score above about 15 indicates enough risk that formal hepatology and transplant evaluation is generally recommended before elective nonhepatic surgery. Correcting the INR alone does not change the underlying risk, and MELD predicts postoperative mortality in nonhepatic surgery as well.

questions.stem: Three patients have Child-Pugh scores of 6, 8, and 12. Which patient has the most compensated disease and the lowest operative risk?
questions.explanation: Child-Pugh class A, 5 to 6 points, represents compensated cirrhosis with the lowest operative risk. Class B, 7 to 9 points, carries moderate risk, and class C, 10 to 15 points, is decompensated disease with very high perioperative mortality.

questions.stem: A patient with Child-Pugh C cirrhosis has ascites, encephalopathy, bilirubin 4.2, albumin 2.4, and INR 2.1 and requests elective hernia repair. Which recommendation best follows the risk stratification?
